ssh_server.exposure: Heavily targeted by automated scanners and brute-force attacks — internet-exposed by default
ssh_server.threat: Full shell access to the machine, privilege escalation, lateral movement to other network systems

vnc_server.exposure: Often lacks native encryption; weak or absent authentication on older versions
vnc_server.threat: Full visual and interactive desktop control — equivalent to physical access to the machine

ftp_server.exposure: Unencrypted protocol — credentials and data transmitted in plain text over the network
ftp_server.threat: Credential theft, file access and exfiltration, potential pivot if credentials are reused

postgresql.exposure: Password or configurable authentication — direct exposure is rarely intentional
postgresql.threat: Full database exfiltration, system command execution via extensions (pg_execute_server_program)

redis.exposure: No authentication by default historically, very frequently misconfigured and exposed
redis.threat: Read/write access to all data, remote code execution (RCE) via configuration — documented and actively exploited attack vector

wireguard_vpn.exposure: Intentionally internet-facing for VPN function — limited attack surface by design
wireguard_vpn.threat: Full internal network access if tunnel is compromised or private keys are stolen

home_assistant.exposure: Web interface controlling physical devices — built-in authentication but often exposed for remote access
home_assistant.threat: Control of physical devices (locks, alarms, switches), local network access via automations, home automation data exfiltration

nextcloud.exposure: Personal file server exposed to the internet — authentication required but significant attack surface depending on installed apps
nextcloud.threat: Access to all personal files, contacts and calendars stored, potential pivot if credentials are compromised

samba_windows_file_sharing.exposure: Designed exclusively for local networks — inherently dangerous if exposed to the internet
samba_windows_file_sharing.threat: File access and encryption (ransomware), lateral movement (EternalBlue/WannaCry), data exfiltration

mysql___mariadb.exposure: Password-based authentication, history of unauthenticated access CVEs
mysql___mariadb.threat: Full database exfiltration, data destruction, application-level access if credentials are shared

cockpit_web_admin.exposure: Web-based system administration interface — authentication required but significant attack surface
cockpit_web_admin.threat: Full system administration if compromised: service management, users, network, root terminal

mosquitto_mqtt.exposure: MQTT broker often without authentication by default, listens on all interfaces
mosquitto_mqtt.threat: Unauthorised publish/subscribe to home automation topics, device control, sensor data interception

apache_web_server.exposure: Web server potentially exposed to the internet — commonly targeted by automated vulnerability scanners
apache_web_server.threat: Web application exploits, path traversal, remote code execution if CGI or modules are misconfigured

nginx_web_server.exposure: Web server potentially exposed to the internet — commonly targeted by automated vulnerability scanners
nginx_web_server.threat: Web application exploits, reverse proxy misconfigurations leading to internal service exposure

transmission_web_ui.exposure: Web interface for BitTorrent client — unauthenticated access by default on older versions
transmission_web_ui.threat: Remote control of downloads, potential RCE via malicious torrents if exposed publicly

qbittorrent_web_ui.exposure: Web interface for BitTorrent client — default credentials (admin/adminadmin) frequently unchanged
qbittorrent_web_ui.threat: Remote control of downloads, file system write access via download directory configuration

avahi_local_network_discovery.exposure: mDNS/DNS-SD service — designed for local network use only, not internet-facing
avahi_local_network_discovery.threat: Local network device and service enumeration — low risk on isolated or properly firewalled networks

cups_network_printing.exposure: Print server — typically restricted to local network, not intended for internet exposure
cups_network_printing.threat: Printer access and configuration disclosure on local network — minimal risk if not publicly exposed

jellyfin.exposure: Media server web interface — may be exposed for remote streaming access
jellyfin.threat: Unauthorised media access, potential RCE if outdated versions with known CVEs are running

plex_media_server.exposure: Media server with cloud relay — phone-home by default, may be directly accessible if port-forwarded
plex_media_server.threat: Unauthorised media access, metadata exposure, potential RCE on outdated versions

gitea.exposure: Self-hosted Git service — may contain private repositories, credentials and CI/CD secrets
gitea.threat: Source code and secret exfiltration, arbitrary code execution via Git hooks if admin account is compromised

syncthing.exposure: Peer-to-peer file sync — web UI bound to localhost by default, sync protocol may be externally reachable
syncthing.threat: File access and modification, directory traversal if misconfigured, data synchronisation interception

telnet_server.exposure: Unencrypted plaintext protocol — credentials, commands and all data transmitted in clear text over the network
telnet_server.threat: Credential theft in transit, session hijacking, trivial interception on any network segment — replace with SSH immediately

rdp___xrdp.exposure: Remote desktop protocol — primary target of ransomware operators and automated scanners (BlueKeep, DejaBlue CVEs)
rdp___xrdp.threat: Full graphical desktop access, credential theft, ransomware deployment, lateral movement to other systems

mongodb.exposure: No authentication by default in older versions — hundreds of thousands of unprotected instances found publicly exposed
mongodb.threat: Full database read/write access, data exfiltration and destruction, potential code execution via server-side JavaScript

elasticsearch.exposure: No authentication in open-source version by default — frequently misconfigured and indexed publicly by Shodan
elasticsearch.threat: Full exfiltration of all indexed documents, index deletion, cluster takeover — requires X-Pack Security or equivalent

memcached.exposure: No authentication, UDP enabled by default — actively abused for DDoS amplification attacks (factor up to 50,000x)
memcached.threat: Cache poisoning and data exfiltration, amplification DDoS vector against third parties, service disruption

tailscale_vpn.exposure: WireGuard-based encrypted mesh VPN; uses NAT punching, so the daemon typically does not expose a stable listening port to the internet. The control plane authenticates via your identity provider (Google, GitHub, OIDC, etc.).
tailscale_vpn.threat: An attacker who phishes your identity provider account or steals an authenticated session can join your tailnet and reach every node on it. Enable Tailscale ACLs and tags to limit blast radius; require WebAuthn/2FA on the IdP.

caddy_web_server.exposure: HTTP/HTTPS reverse proxy and static site server — internet-exposed by design. Issues TLS via Let's Encrypt automatically.
caddy_web_server.threat: Misconfigured site blocks can leak admin panels or backend services; outdated versions or vulnerable handlers can be exploited. Audit reverse-proxy targets, restrict admin endpoint (port 2019) to localhost, and keep up to date.

adguard_home_dns_sinkhole.exposure: Network-wide DNS server with web admin UI. DNS is reachable by clients (LAN) but the admin UI (3000/tcp) should NEVER be internet-exposed.
adguard_home_dns_sinkhole.threat: Exposed admin UI lets an attacker disable filtering, redirect DNS to malicious resolvers, or read query logs to inventory devices on your network. Bind admin UI to localhost or a private interface and front it with auth.

vaultwarden_password_manager.exposure: Self-hosted password manager API — by design holds every credential the household / team trusts to a third party. Internet-exposed if used for mobile sync from outside the LAN.
vaultwarden_password_manager.threat: Account compromise (master password phish or admin token leak) yields plaintext access to every stored credential — including TOTP seeds. Mandatory: strong admin token rotated quarterly, TLS-only access, fail2ban on /api/accounts/, regular off-site encrypted backups of the data/ directory.

ollama_local_llm.exposure: Local LLM inference daemon. Default listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 but operators frequently bind to 0.0.0.0 to share inference across the LAN — accidentally exposing the API to anyone on the network.
ollama_local_llm.threat: Open API gives any LAN client free inference (compute exhaustion), can extract loaded model files (some are licence-restricted), and historically the API has had path-traversal CVEs allowing arbitrary file read. Keep bound to loopback or a trusted private interface; never expose to the internet.

authelia_sso_auth_proxy.exposure: Authentication portal sitting in front of multiple downstream services — it IS the auth boundary. Internet-exposed by design (mobile users need to authenticate from anywhere).
authelia_sso_auth_proxy.threat: Compromise of the Authelia instance (via a CVE, weak admin password, or storage backend takeover) defeats authentication for every protected service simultaneously. Run on a dedicated host, restrict storage backend access, enable WebAuthn-first auth, and monitor failed-login telemetry.

smtp_server_postfix_exim.exposure: TCP/25 listener accepts mail submissions. Internet-exposed SMTP attracts constant spam relay attempts, SASL credential brute force, and reputation-based scanning. Default postfix configs on Debian/Ubuntu typically bind to 127.0.0.1 only — this finding fires when that default has been changed.
smtp_server_postfix_exim.threat: Open relay abuse blocklists your IP within hours, breaking outbound mail for legitimate users. SASL auth without rate limiting is a slow-motion credential spray target. Misconfigured MTAs have historically been used for spam campaigns at scale and exfiltration channels.

nfs_server.exposure: TCP/UDP 2049 + portmapper (TCP/UDP 111) + statd / lockd dynamic ports. NFSv3 uses host-based authentication (export rules check source IP only), trivially bypassed if the attacker can spoof source or sits on the same untrusted segment.
nfs_server.threat: Read/write access to every exported share for anyone matching the export rule. `no_root_squash` exports allow remote root to write any file (including /etc/sudoers via mounting /). NFSv4 with Kerberos mitigates but is rarely enabled outside enterprise environments.

jenkins.exposure: Web admin UI on TCP/8080 by default — frequently internet-exposed because operators dial in from home. First-boot Jenkins requires a one-time unlock token, and operators routinely leave the resulting instance with weak admin credentials or `Allow anonymous read`.
jenkins.threat: Jenkins is the prime lateral-movement target on most networks: it holds signing keys, deployment credentials, container registry tokens, source-code read access, and the ability to run arbitrary code via build steps. A compromised Jenkins typically owns every downstream system it deploys to.

openvpn.exposure: UDP/1194 by default — must be reachable from client devices, so internet exposure is by design. Well-audited protocol but past CVEs (CVE-2024-37305 buffer overflow, CVE-2024-28882 memory leak) require timely patching.
openvpn.threat: VPN concentrator compromise gives the attacker network access to anything reachable from the VPN subnet — typically the corporate LAN or homelab subnet. Mandatory hardening: TLS-Auth or TLS-Crypt (HMAC over the control channel), strong PKI (no shared static keys), 2FA via PAM, current OpenSSL.

squid_proxy.exposure: TCP/3128 HTTP/HTTPS forward proxy. Should be bound to a private interface with explicit ACLs (`acl localnet src 192.168.1.0/24` etc.). Default config on many distros listens on all interfaces and accepts any client.
squid_proxy.threat: An open forward proxy is rapidly discovered and abused: bandwidth theft (your IP, their downloads), geo-restriction bypass tagged to your IP, anonymisation layer for attacks against third parties (causing your IP to land on abuse blocklists). HTTPS CONNECT tunnels arbitrary TCP, so an open Squid is effectively an open SOCKS proxy.

Run apt update then apt list --upgradable to investigate.

password_auth.title: Password authentication enabled (PasswordAuthentication yes)
password_auth.why: Allows anyone to attempt to guess passwords via brute force. Millions of bots scan the internet 24/7 trying common passwords against SSH port 22. A weak or reused password is all it takes for a full compromise.
password_auth.how:
1. Generate a key pair if you don't have one:
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519
2. Copy your public key to the server:
   ssh-copy-id user@server
3. Disable password auth:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PasswordAuthentication no
4. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

permit_root_login.title: Root SSH login permitted (PermitRootLogin)
permit_root_login.why: Direct root login bypasses audit trails and gives full system access from the first connection. If an attacker guesses or steals the root credential, no further privilege escalation is needed — the server is fully compromised immediately.
permit_root_login.how:
1. Ensure a regular user with sudo rights exists
2. Disable root login:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PermitRootLogin no
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

permit_empty_passwords.title: Empty passwords allowed (PermitEmptyPasswords yes)
permit_empty_passwords.why: Any account without a password is directly accessible over SSH with a blank password. This is an immediate full-access vulnerability requiring zero effort from an attacker.
permit_empty_passwords.how:
1. Disable empty passwords:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PermitEmptyPasswords no
2. Lock accounts with empty passwords:
   sudo passwd -l <username>
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

allow_tcp_forwarding.title: TCP forwarding enabled (AllowTcpForwarding yes)
allow_tcp_forwarding.why: TCP forwarding lets any authenticated user tunnel arbitrary TCP traffic through SSH. An attacker with a valid account can pivot to internal services that are not directly reachable from the internet.
allow_tcp_forwarding.how:
1. Disable TCP forwarding:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  AllowTcpForwarding no
2. If specific users need port forwarding, use:
   AllowTcpForwarding local
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

pubkey_auth_disabled.title: Public key authentication disabled (PubkeyAuthentication no)
pubkey_auth_disabled.why: Disabling public key authentication forces all users onto password login. This removes the strongest authentication mechanism available and makes the server entirely dependent on password strength.
pubkey_auth_disabled.how:
1. Enable key-based authentication:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PubkeyAuthentication yes
2. Generate a key pair:
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519
3. Copy the key to the server:
   ssh-copy-id user@server
4. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

dsa_key.title: DSA host key in use
dsa_key.why: DSA keys are cryptographically broken and deprecated in OpenSSH 7.0+. The algorithm offers only 1024-bit security and is vulnerable to attacks when the random number generator produces weak values.
dsa_key.how:
1. Remove the DSA host key:
   sudo rm /etc/ssh/ssh_host_dsa_key*
2. Regenerate all host keys:
   sudo ssh-keygen -A
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh
4. Remove old fingerprints from clients:
   ssh-keygen -R <hostname>

no_passphrase.title: Private key without passphrase
no_passphrase.why: If the key file is copied or stolen — via a compromised server, backup leak, or misconfigured storage — the attacker gains immediate access to every system that trusts it. No cracking required.
no_passphrase.how:
1. Add a passphrase to an existing key:
   ssh-keygen -p -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
2. Use ssh-agent to avoid re-entering the passphrase every session
3. For service accounts, use dedicated keys with restrictive authorized_keys options (command=, from=)

client_strict_host_no.title: StrictHostKeyChecking disabled in SSH client config
client_strict_host_no.why: Disabling host verification allows man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks: an attacker can silently intercept your SSH session and impersonate the server with no warning displayed.
client_strict_host_no.how:
1. Remove StrictHostKeyChecking no from ~/.ssh/config
2. Use the default: StrictHostKeyChecking ask (first connection prompts, subsequent connections verify)
3. To skip verification for one specific host only, use a Host block:
   Host jump-host.example.com
       StrictHostKeyChecking no

ignore_rhosts_disabled.title: IgnoreRhosts disabled — .rhosts files trusted
ignore_rhosts_disabled.why: .rhosts files allow passwordless login based on hostname alone. Hostnames can be spoofed, making this a trivial authentication bypass that has been obsolete for decades.
ignore_rhosts_disabled.how:
1. Enable IgnoreRhosts (the default):
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  IgnoreRhosts yes
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

host_based_auth.title: Host-based authentication enabled
host_based_auth.why: Host-based authentication trusts the identity of a remote host rather than a user credential. If the trusted host is compromised, attackers automatically gain access to this server without any further authentication.
host_based_auth.how:
1. Disable host-based authentication (the default):
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  HostbasedAuthentication no
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

strict_modes_disabled.title: SSH StrictModes disabled
strict_modes_disabled.why: Without StrictModes, sshd skips permission checks on ~/.ssh and key files. World-readable private keys or group-writable home directories are silently accepted, effectively nullifying file permission security.
strict_modes_disabled.how:
1. Enable StrictModes (the default):
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  StrictModes yes
2. Fix file permissions:
   chmod 700 ~/.ssh
   chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

max_auth_tries.title: Too many authentication attempts allowed (MaxAuthTries > 3)
max_auth_tries.why: Each failed SSH attempt can probe valid usernames and test credentials. With the default of 6 attempts, an automated attack can test many passwords per connection before being disconnected. Reducing to 3 limits the credential surface per connection and makes brute-force campaigns significantly slower.
max_auth_tries.how:
1. Reduce MaxAuthTries:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  MaxAuthTries 3
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

permit_user_env.title: User environment variables allowed (PermitUserEnvironment yes)
permit_user_env.why: Allowing users to set environment variables via ~/.ssh/environment or authorized_keys options enables privilege escalation through environment manipulation: LD_PRELOAD, PATH, or PYTHONPATH overrides can redirect execution to attacker-controlled code even when the binary is trusted.
permit_user_env.how:
1. Disable user environment:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PermitUserEnvironment no
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

weak_ciphers.title: Weak SSH cipher suites in use
weak_ciphers.why: Legacy ciphers (3DES-CBC, arcfour/RC4, blowfish-CBC, CBC-mode AES) are cryptographically weak or broken. CBC-mode ciphers are vulnerable to BEAST and Lucky13 attacks. RC4 has statistical biases exploitable with enough traffic. An attacker recording sessions could later decrypt them.
weak_ciphers.how:
1. Restrict to strong ciphers:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
   Ciphers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com,aes128-gcm@openssh.com,aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh
3. Test your client still connects:
   ssh -Q cipher  # lists supported ciphers

weak_macs.title: Weak SSH MAC algorithms in use
weak_macs.why: Weak MACs (hmac-md5, hmac-sha1, umac-64) are vulnerable to collision attacks. A compromised MAC means message integrity cannot be guaranteed — an attacker in a man-in-the-middle position could tamper with session data in transit without detection. MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer collision-resistant.
weak_macs.how:
1. Restrict to strong MACs:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
   MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com,umac-128-etm@openssh.com
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

weak_kex.title: Weak SSH key exchange algorithms in use
weak_kex.why: Weak KEX algorithms (diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 uses a 1024-bit group; diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 uses deprecated SHA-1) offer insufficient forward secrecy. Nation-state actors have demonstrated precomputation attacks against standard 1024-bit DH groups (Logjam). Compromised KEX means the session key can be recovered after the fact.
weak_kex.how:
1. Restrict to strong KEX:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
   KexAlgorithms curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org,diffie-hellman-group16-sha512,diffie-hellman-group18-sha512
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

rsa_weak.title: RSA host key too short (< 4096 bits)
rsa_weak.why: RSA keys shorter than 4096 bits are considered weak by modern cryptographic standards. As computing power increases and factorisation attacks improve, short keys become feasible to break. Keys under 2048 bits are practically broken today.
rsa_weak.how:
1. Generate a new 4096-bit RSA host key:
   sudo ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key -N ''
2. Or prefer Ed25519 (shorter but stronger):
   sudo ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key -N ''
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh
4. Remove old host fingerprints on clients:
   ssh-keygen -R <hostname>

login_grace_time.title: LoginGraceTime too long (> 60s)
login_grace_time.why: A long grace period keeps unauthenticated TCP connections open for longer than necessary. An attacker can hold open many parallel SSH connections without completing authentication, potentially exhausting connection limits and degrading service for legitimate users.
login_grace_time.how:
1. Reduce LoginGraceTime:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  LoginGraceTime 30
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

no_allow_users.title: No AllowUsers / AllowGroups restriction in SSH config
no_allow_users.why: Without AllowUsers or AllowGroups, every system account with a valid credential can attempt SSH login — including service accounts, daemon users, and legacy accounts not intended for remote access. Restricting SSH to specific users dramatically reduces the attack surface.
no_allow_users.how:
1. Decide which users or groups need SSH access
2. Add an AllowUsers directive:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  AllowUsers alice bob deploy
3. Or restrict by group:
   AllowGroups sshusers
   sudo addgroup sshusers && sudo adduser alice sshusers
4. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

private_key_perms.title: SSH private key file permissions too open
private_key_perms.why: Private keys must be readable only by their owner (mode 0600). If group- or world-readable, any user sharing the same group — or any user on the system — can read the key and impersonate whoever owns it on every server that trusts it.
private_key_perms.how:
1. Restrict permissions:
   chmod 600 <key_path>
2. Verify ownership:
   ls -la <key_path>  →  -rw------- owner owner
3. For root-owned host keys:
   sudo chmod 600 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key

authorized_keys_perms.title: authorized_keys file permissions too open
authorized_keys_perms.why: An authorized_keys file writable by others allows any user who can write to it to inject their own public key and gain SSH access as this account. Read access by others leaks information about who is authorised and from which hosts.
authorized_keys_perms.how:
1. Restrict permissions:
   chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
2. Verify ownership matches the account:
   ls -la ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
3. Enable StrictModes in sshd_config to enforce permission checks automatically:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  StrictModes yes

authorized_keys_dsa.title: DSA key in authorized_keys
authorized_keys_dsa.why: DSA keys use a cryptographically broken algorithm, deprecated in OpenSSH 7.0+. They offer only 1024-bit security and authentication via a DSA key provides weaker guarantees than any modern alternative.
authorized_keys_dsa.how:
1. Identify the DSA key line (starts with 'ssh-dss')
2. Remove it from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
3. Ask the key owner to generate a new key:
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519
4. Add the new public key to authorized_keys
5. Confirm removal:
   grep 'ssh-dss' ~/.ssh/authorized_keys  # should return nothing

authorized_keys_weak_key.title: Weak RSA key in authorized_keys (< 4096 bits)
authorized_keys_weak_key.why: Short RSA keys in authorized_keys are as dangerous as weak host keys: an attacker who factors the private key gains permanent backdoor access to this account on every server that trusts it — including this one.
authorized_keys_weak_key.how:
1. Identify weak RSA keys (ssh-rsa entries with a short modulus)
2. Ask the key owner to generate a stronger key:
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519  # or: ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096
3. Replace the weak entry in authorized_keys with the new public key
4. Revoke the old key from all servers it was used on

authorized_keys_no_restrictions.title: authorized_keys entries without command or host restrictions
authorized_keys_no_restrictions.why: authorized_keys supports options (command=, from=, restrict) that limit what a key can do and from where. Without restrictions, a compromised key grants unrestricted shell access from any IP. For service or deployment keys this violates the principle of least privilege.
authorized_keys_no_restrictions.how:
1. For service keys, add a command= restriction:
   command="/usr/bin/rsync --server ...",no-pty,no-agent-forwarding ssh-ed25519 AAAA...
2. For keys from known sources, add a from= restriction:
   from="192.168.1.0/24" ssh-ed25519 AAAA...
3. Use the restrict option to disable all optional features:
   restrict,command="..." ssh-ed25519 AAAA...

authorized_keys_duplicate.title: Duplicate entries in authorized_keys
authorized_keys_duplicate.why: Duplicate keys suggest the file was modified without proper housekeeping — potentially by automation or by a user who lost track of what was added. Stale duplicates may belong to revoked users or compromised credentials that were never cleaned up.
authorized_keys_duplicate.how:
1. De-duplicate authorized_keys:
   sort -u ~/.ssh/authorized_keys > /tmp/ak_clean && mv /tmp/ak_clean ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
2. Review each key comment to verify it belongs to an active, authorised user
3. Remove any key whose owner is no longer authorised

dir_perms.title: ~/.ssh directory permissions too open
dir_perms.why: The ~/.ssh directory must be mode 0700 (owner only). If group- or world-readable, any user on the system can enumerate authorized_keys, known_hosts, and discover which systems this account can access. If writable, they can inject their own public key.
dir_perms.how:
1. Fix directory permissions:
   chmod 700 ~/.ssh
2. Fix all files inside:
   chmod 600 ~/.ssh/*
   chmod 644 ~/.ssh/*.pub 2>/dev/null; true
3. Verify:
   ls -la ~ | grep .ssh  →  drwx------

client_forward_agent.title: SSH agent forwarding enabled in client config (ForwardAgent yes)
client_forward_agent.why: Agent forwarding passes your SSH authentication credentials through to the remote server. If that server is compromised, root on that server can use your agent to authenticate as you on any other server your key grants access to — without ever seeing your private key.
client_forward_agent.how:
1. Disable agent forwarding globally:
   nano ~/.ssh/config  →  ForwardAgent no
2. Enable it only for specific trusted jump hosts where strictly necessary:
   Host jump.trusted.example.com
       ForwardAgent yes
3. Prefer ProxyJump for chaining SSH connections instead of agent forwarding

client_known_hosts_devnull.title: SSH client known_hosts pointed to /dev/null
client_known_hosts_devnull.why: Pointing known_hosts to /dev/null disables host key verification entirely. Every SSH connection silently accepts any host key — including a man-in-the-middle attacker presenting a forged key. This is equivalent to never verifying server identity.
client_known_hosts_devnull.how:
1. Remove the UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null line from ~/.ssh/config
2. Let SSH use its default: ~/.ssh/known_hosts
3. On first connection to each host, verify the fingerprint out-of-band before accepting it

known_hosts_deprecated.title: Deprecated key type in known_hosts
known_hosts_deprecated.why: Entries in known_hosts using deprecated algorithms (DSA, short RSA) provide weak integrity guarantees for host verification. If an attacker can forge a key of that type, they can impersonate the target host without triggering a warning.
known_hosts_deprecated.how:
1. Remove the deprecated entry:
   ssh-keygen -R <hostname>
2. Reconnect to the server — SSH will re-add it with its current key type
3. Ask the server admin to ensure only Ed25519 or RSA-4096 host keys are active

known_hosts_duplicate.title: Duplicate entries in known_hosts
known_hosts_duplicate.why: Multiple entries for the same host with different keys can cause confusion and may allow SSH to silently accept a stale or compromised key. It also indicates the file has not been maintained.
known_hosts_duplicate.how:
1. Remove all entries for the affected host:
   ssh-keygen -R <hostname>
2. Reconnect to add a single clean entry
3. Periodically clean known_hosts of stale entries for decommissioned hosts

host_key_dsa.title: SSH host key uses DSA (deprecated and considered insecure)
host_key_dsa.why: DSA host keys are limited to 1024 bits and use a signature algorithm vulnerable to nonce-reuse attacks. OpenSSH dropped support for DSA host keys by default in version 7.0 (2015) — modern clients refuse to connect to a server presenting only a DSA host key. The key being present means the host was either upgraded from a very old install or somebody intentionally re-enabled DSA. Either way, the cryptographic posture is weak.
host_key_dsa.how:
1. Generate a modern host key (ed25519, the recommended choice for new keys):
   sudo ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key -N ''
2. Ensure sshd_config does NOT include the DSA key (remove or comment out):
   HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh_host_dsa_key   # <-- remove this line
3. Remove the DSA key files:
   sudo rm /etc/ssh/ssh_host_dsa_key /etc/ssh/ssh_host_dsa_key.pub
4. Restart sshd:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh
Note: existing SSH clients will see a 'host key changed' warning the first time after key removal. Communicate the change to legitimate users.

server.why: On any server, DSA host keys should not exist in 2026. Generate ed25519 (and optionally RSA-4096 for legacy client compatibility), remove DSA, restart sshd.

desktop.why: Desktop SSH servers are less common but the same hygiene applies. Replace DSA with ed25519 if SSH is reachable at all.

container.why: Containerised SSH typically generates fresh keys at first boot. If DSA is present in a container image, regenerate with ed25519 at image build time.

not_active.title: SSH server is installed but the sshd service is not running
not_active.why: The openssh-server package is installed but sshd is not active — operators cannot connect via SSH. Whether this is a problem depends on intent. On a server, SSH is typically the primary administration channel — having it dormant after a reboot means a console drive is required to recover access. On a desktop without remote management, an inactive sshd is the safe state and the package could simply be uninstalled.
not_active.how:
If SSH IS wanted (typical for servers):
1. Start and enable the service:
   sudo systemctl enable --now ssh
2. Verify it is listening:
   ss -tlnp | grep :22
3. Confirm authentication works from a known-good client.
If SSH is NOT wanted (typical for non-administered desktops):
1. Stop and disable cleanly:
   sudo systemctl disable --now ssh
2. Optional — remove the package entirely:
   sudo apt remove --purge openssh-server

server.why: On a server, an inactive sshd typically means a maintenance session was not reversed. Re-enable; without SSH, the next remote intervention requires hardware console access.

desktop.why: On a desktop where SSH is not used, the safe state is to uninstall openssh-server entirely rather than leaving it installed-but-disabled — that keeps the attack surface from re-appearing after a future reboot or update.

container.why: Most container images should NOT run SSH (use docker exec / kubectl exec / podman exec instead). If sshd is installed but inactive in a container, consider removing it from the image.

server.title: X11 forwarding enabled (X11Forwarding yes)
server.why: X11 forwarding exposes your local X11 display to a remote server. A malicious or compromised remote host could capture keystrokes and screen contents from your X session.
server.how:
1. Disable X11 forwarding:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  X11Forwarding no
2. If genuinely needed, ensure X11UseLocalhost yes is also set
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

client.title: Client X11 forwarding enabled (ForwardX11 yes)
client.why: When you connect with `ssh -X` or have `ForwardX11 yes` in ~/.ssh/config, your local X server is exposed to the remote host through an SSH tunnel. A malicious or compromised remote can take screenshots of your local desktop, inject keystrokes into any X application, and read your clipboard — the X11 protocol has no security boundary between local and forwarded applications.
client.how:
1. Open ~/.ssh/config:
   nano ~/.ssh/config
2. Remove or set to 'no' any 'ForwardX11 yes' lines
3. If X11 forwarding is genuinely needed for specific hosts, restrict it per-Host block and prefer 'ForwardX11Trusted no' (use the SECURITY extension to limit remote access)
4. Use 'ssh -X host' on-demand only for trusted hosts where you need a one-shot graphical app

world_writable.title: World-writable sensitive file
world_writable.why: Any local user on the system can modify this file. For configuration files (sshd_config, sudoers) this allows privilege escalation. For credential files it allows tampering that persists across sessions.
world_writable.how:
1. Identify the file and owner:
   ls -la <path>
2. Remove world-write permission:
   sudo chmod o-w <path>
3. Verify the fix:
   ls -la <path>  →  last three bits should be ---

too_permissive.title: File permissions too open
too_permissive.why: Overly permissive files can be read or written by unintended users. SSH keys readable by others allow impersonation. Configuration files readable by all may leak credentials or internal paths.
too_permissive.how:
1. Note the expected permissions shown in the audit output
2. Apply the correct permissions:
   sudo chmod <expected> <path>
3. Verify:
   ls -la <path>

sudoers_nopasswd_all.title: NOPASSWD:ALL in sudoers (unrestricted passwordless sudo)
sudoers_nopasswd_all.why: Grants full, unrestricted root access without any password. If this account is compromised — malware, stolen session token, weak password — the attacker has immediate full system control with zero additional effort.
sudoers_nopasswd_all.how:
1. Edit sudoers safely:
   sudo visudo
2. Replace NOPASSWD:ALL with a specific command list, e.g.:
   user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/apt-get
3. If passwordless sudo is needed for automation, isolate it to a dedicated service account with a minimal allowed command list

ssh_host_key_perms.title: SSH host key permissions too open
ssh_host_key_perms.why: SSH host private keys must be readable only by root. If a non-root user can read the host key, they can impersonate this server to any client — enabling a man-in-the-middle attack on future SSH connections.
ssh_host_key_perms.how:
1. Restrict permissions:
   sudo chmod 600 <path>
2. Verify root ownership:
   sudo chown root:root <path>
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

security_pending.title: Security updates pending
security_pending.why: Pending security updates mean the system contains known vulnerabilities with public CVEs and often public exploits. Attackers actively scan for unpatched systems. Every day of delay increases the window of exposure.
security_pending.how:
1. Apply security updates now:
   sudo apt-get upgrade
2. Preview what would be applied:
   sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run
3. Apply only security patches automatically:
   sudo unattended-upgrade
4. If kernel updates are included, reboot:
   sudo reboot

server.why: Pending security updates on a server create known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Attackers prioritise recently-published CVEs where patches exist but have not been applied — this is the most common attack vector on public-facing servers. Apply updates immediately.

desktop.why: Pending security updates affect all profiles, but on a desktop the most critical are kernel, browser, and library updates that handle untrusted input. Apply them promptly to protect against local privilege escalation and drive-by attack vectors.

container.why: In a container, pending updates should be addressed by rebuilding the image from an updated base rather than running apt inside the container. Running apt upgrade in a running container is a temporary workaround — the correct solution is updating your Dockerfile base image and redeploying.
container.how:
Rebuild from an updated base image:
   # Update your Dockerfile's FROM tag or use --pull to get the latest:
   docker build --pull -t <your-image> .
   docker compose up -d
For an immediate stop-gap only:
   docker exec -it <container> apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y

unattended_not_configured.title: Automatic security updates not configured
unattended_not_configured.why: Without automatic updates, security patches accumulate until someone manually applies them. Maintenance windows of exposure grow over time, and critical patches are often missed on servers without active monitoring.
unattended_not_configured.how:
1. Install the package:
   sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
2. Configure it interactively:
   sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades
3. Verify the service is active:
   sudo systemctl status unattended-upgrades
4. Test with a dry run:
   sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run -d

server.why: On an exposed server, every unpatched day is an open window. Attackers actively scan for systems missing recent CVEs. Manual update management on a server almost always means patches lag — automatic security updates are non-negotiable on public-facing infrastructure.

desktop.why: On a desktop, manual update management is common and acceptable. The risk is lower since no inbound services are publicly exposed. However, delaying security patches for more than a week increases local privilege escalation and browser/library exploit risk.

container.why: In a container environment, updates are managed at the image level — not via unattended-upgrades. If your pipeline regularly rebuilds from an updated base image, this finding does not apply. Verify your CI/CD includes base image refresh.
container.how:
Rebuild the image from an updated base rather than running apt inside the container:
   # Update your Dockerfile base image tag, then:
   docker build --pull -t <your-image> .
   docker compose up -d
For the host system (if unattended-upgrades is needed there):
   sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
   sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

apt_cache_stale.title: APT cache is stale (apt update has not run recently)
apt_cache_stale.why: `apt-get -s upgrade` reports against the local package cache, not what is actually available on the upstream repositories. When the cache is several days old, BOB's 'no updates pending' message reflects an outdated view of what is actually patchable — the system may have dozens of pending security updates upstream that have not yet been advertised locally. This is the same failure mode that produced false 'system up to date' verdicts on fresh Ubuntu VMs (v0.4.4 cross-distro terrain test).
apt_cache_stale.how:
1. Refresh the cache now:
   sudo apt update
2. Schedule daily updates of the cache itself (NOT the upgrade — see unattended_not_configured for that):
   # systemd-based distros usually already enable apt-daily.timer:
   systemctl status apt-daily.timer
   sudo systemctl enable --now apt-daily.timer
3. Verify the cache is fresh:
   stat /var/cache/apt/pkgcache.bin   # mtime should be within the last day

server.why: On a server, a stale cache hides pending security patches. apt-daily.timer should be enabled — verify it actually fires (the most common reason for stale caches is a timer left disabled by a hardening script).

desktop.why: Desktops often go offline for extended periods (laptops, kiosks). After coming back online, run `apt update` once before trusting any 'up to date' verdict.

container.why: Container caches age with the image. Rebuild the image regularly or include `apt update && apt upgrade` in the build step to avoid shipping stale catalogues.

dist_upgrade_inconsistent.title: apt-get upgrade and apt-get dist-upgrade report different update counts
dist_upgrade_inconsistent.why: `apt-get -s upgrade` is conservative — it refuses to install any package that would require installing a new dependency or removing an existing one. `apt-get -s dist-upgrade` is more aggressive and resolves these dependency changes. When the two disagree, it usually means kernel updates, library version bumps, or transitively-pulled new packages are pending but not visible in the conservative output. The user sees 'no updates' from apt-get upgrade and misses real security patches that dist-upgrade would have applied.
dist_upgrade_inconsistent.how:
1. Inspect what dist-upgrade would do:
   sudo apt-get -s dist-upgrade
2. If the difference is mostly kernel-related, apply via apt full-upgrade:
   sudo apt full-upgrade
   sudo reboot   # required after kernel upgrade
3. For unattended-upgrades, switch the package list from `upgrade` to `dist-upgrade` semantics:
   sudo nano /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades
   Unattended-Upgrade::OnlyOnACPower "false";   # for laptops if needed
4. Re-verify:
   sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade --dry-run

server.why: On a server, conservative `apt upgrade` masks kernel and library updates that dist-upgrade would apply. Use full-upgrade for routine patching and reboot during maintenance windows.

desktop.why: Desktop users often run `apt upgrade` from habit. Periodically run `apt full-upgrade` to catch pending kernel and library updates that the conservative variant skips.

container.why: Containers do not normally apply runtime upgrades — rebuild the base image to pick up new package versions.

journald_volatile.title: systemd-journald is configured for volatile storage (logs lost on reboot)
journald_volatile.why: systemd-journald's default `Storage=auto` becomes volatile when /var/log/journal/ does not exist — logs live in RAM and are erased on every reboot. Forensic investigations after an incident depend on log history; if the journal is volatile, restart-related evidence (boot messages, login attempts, service crashes) is gone the moment the machine comes back up. The journal also fills RAM rather than disk, which is a performance issue under high log volume.
journald_volatile.how:
1. Create the persistent journal directory:
   sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal
2. systemd-journald will detect it automatically on next start. To pick up the change immediately:
   sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal
   sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
3. Verify persistent storage is now active:
   journalctl --header | grep 'Storage'
4. Confirm new logs survive a reboot:
   sudo reboot   # then 'journalctl --since=yesterday'

server.why: On a server, volatile journal = no forensic evidence after a reboot. Always run with persistent storage. Even a single boot loop wipes the prior journal.

desktop.why: Desktops reboot frequently; volatile journal makes troubleshooting service issues much harder. Enable persistence.

container.why: Container journals depend on the runtime's log handling. Address at the runtime level (Docker, podman, kubelet) — host journal persistence is a host concern.

logrotate_missing.title: logrotate is missing or has no active configuration files
logrotate_missing.why: Without logrotate, log files in /var/log/ grow without limit. On systems with verbose services (web servers, auth log floods from SSH brute-force, application stack traces) the disk can fill in days, taking the host offline. The most common cause is a custom distro install where the logrotate package was excluded, or a recently-purged install that took the configuration with it.
logrotate_missing.how:
1. Install logrotate:
   sudo apt install logrotate
2. Verify the default rotation directory has rules:
   ls /etc/logrotate.d/
3. (Optional) Re-create rules for any package that should have shipped one:
   sudo dpkg-reconfigure <package>
4. Test rotation manually:
   sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.conf   # dry-run with verbose output
   sudo logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.conf   # force rotation now

server.why: On a server, missing logrotate is a slow-motion outage waiting to happen — the disk fills, the host crashes. Install + verify the daily cron entry exists.

desktop.why: On a desktop, the disk impact is slower but still real. Verify logrotate is installed; if you're tight on disk, set tighter rotation policies.

container.why: Containers typically rely on the runtime to manage log output (json-file driver, journald driver, etc.), not logrotate. If logrotate is missing in a long-running container, that's a deviation from standard practice — but the fix is rarely 'install logrotate', it's 'use the runtime's log driver'.

brute_found.title: UFW logs show signs of an active brute-force attempt
brute_found.why: BOB's UFW log analyser detected one or more source IPs hitting a single service port with high frequency — a brute-force signature. Whether the source is automated (botnet scanner) or targeted (an actor specifically interested in this host) does not change the action: the brute-force attempt indicates the service is exposed to clients you cannot trust, and rate limiting or geographic restriction is overdue. The finding usually fires on SSH but can also surface on SMTP, IMAP, web admin panels and any other authenticated service.
brute_found.how:
Layered response:
1. Install fail2ban if not present and enable the jail for the targeted service (sshd is the most common):
   sudo apt install fail2ban
   sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
   sudo nano /etc/fail2ban/jail.local   # ensure the relevant jail has enabled=true
2. Restrict the service to known IPs at the firewall layer:
   sudo ufw allow from <trusted-ip> to any port 22
   sudo ufw delete allow 22   # if a broader rule existed
3. For SSH specifically, disable password auth (force pubkey only):
   sudo sed -i 's/^#*PasswordAuthentication yes/PasswordAuthentication no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

server.why: On a public-facing server, brute force attempts are constant. fail2ban + key-only SSH is the baseline. Without either, account compromise is a matter of time.

desktop.why: Brute force on a desktop typically means the machine is exposed in a way it should not be (port-forwarded SSH on a residential router, public Wi-Fi). Close the exposure rather than relying solely on fail2ban.

container.why: Container exposure flows through the host. Address at the host UFW + fail2ban layer; restrict the container's publish address.

exposed.title: SMTP listener is reachable from outside the host (not bound to 127.0.0.1)
exposed.why: Most SMTP services (postfix, sendmail, exim) are configured to accept local-only mail submissions for system notifications. When the listener binds to 0.0.0.0 or a public interface instead of 127.0.0.1, the machine becomes a candidate for relay abuse (spam senders bouncing through it) and for direct brute-force attempts against SASL authentication. SMTP on the open internet is one of the highest-noise attack surfaces; bots probe every IP with open 25/tcp constantly.
exposed.how:
1. Determine which interface the SMTP daemon binds to:
   ss -tlnp | grep :25
2. Restrict to localhost — for postfix:
   sudo postconf -e 'inet_interfaces = loopback-only'
   sudo systemctl restart postfix
   # for sendmail / exim, edit the relevant config (sendmail.cf / exim4.conf) similarly
3. If outbound mail is needed but inbound is not, this is the correct posture — local apps submit via 127.0.0.1, outbound goes via a relay.
4. If inbound SMTP is intentional (mail server role), tighten authentication (SASL with strong creds, TLS-only) and consider rate-limiting at the firewall.

server.why: On a server, internet-exposed SMTP that is not intentionally a mail server invites relay abuse and credential brute force. Bind to loopback unless this machine genuinely is a public mail host.

desktop.why: On a desktop, SMTP exposure is almost always accidental (postfix installed by a meta-package and configured for all interfaces by default). Bind to loopback.

container.why: Mail containers should bind to the container network only and be reachable through an explicit reverse-proxy or relay, not directly published.

no_backup.title: No backup solution detected (timeshift, restic, borg, etc.)
no_backup.why: Without a backup tool, recovery from ransomware, hardware failure, accidental deletion, or filesystem corruption is impossible. The cost of a single bad day far exceeds the cost of any backup solution. The check is not 'is the backup recent' — BOB cannot evaluate that — but 'is a backup tool even installed', which is a baseline configuration question.
no_backup.how:
Pick a tool that matches your storage target:
1. Local snapshots (laptop, single workstation) — timeshift is the simplest:
   sudo apt install timeshift
   sudo timeshift --create --comments 'initial baseline'
2. Off-site / encrypted (server, NAS target) — restic or borg:
   sudo apt install restic
   restic init -r <backup-location>
   restic backup -r <backup-location> /etc /home
3. Whichever tool: schedule via systemd timer or cron, and TEST a restore at least once. Untested backups are not backups.

server.why: On a server, no backup means a single disk failure or successful ransomware encryption is an unrecoverable incident. Pick restic / borg with an off-site target and verify restore quarterly.

desktop.why: On a desktop, even a basic timeshift snapshot lets you roll back after a botched update. The bar is low; install something.

container.why: Container hosts need host-level backup; data volumes need explicit volume backup. Containers themselves should be rebuildable from images — the data is what matters.

sensitive_remote.title: Sensitive service is reachable from the public internet (high-criticality risk)
sensitive_remote.why: A service rated high or critical in the BOB service registry (ssh, samba, telnet, …) has an open TCP listener AND the network context indicates the host is publicly addressable (no NAT, no LAN-only firewall). The combination means the service is one bot scan away from being targeted — and for high-risk services like ssh, samba or rdp, the active threat is brute-forcing creds, exploiting known CVEs, and lateral movement after compromise.
sensitive_remote.how:
Apply in order of impact:
1. Move the service off the public internet entirely (VPN, WireGuard, jump host):
   sudo apt install wireguard
   # configure WG, then bind the sensitive service to the wg interface only
2. If public exposure is genuinely required, harden the service:
   - SSH: key-only auth, no root login, fail2ban, port knocking or change-port-from-22 (security through obscurity helps against bot noise even if not real protection).
   - Samba: restrict to source IPs at UFW + 'hosts allow' in smb.conf; SMB on the internet is a CVE waiting to be exploited.
   - Telnet/RDP: do not expose. Migrate to ssh/RDP-over-VPN.
3. Add an external monitoring alert for unexpected connections.

server.why: On a public server, sensitive services on the open internet are the primary entry vector for most compromises. VPN-front the admin services and keep only the application's actual public ports exposed.

desktop.why: A desktop with a sensitive port on the public internet is almost always a misconfiguration (a port-forward someone added years ago and forgot). Audit your router's port-forward table and close anything you don't actively need.

container.why: Container ports published to 0.0.0.0 inherit the host's public exposure. Bind to 127.0.0.1 or a private interface, or front the container with a VPN.

rp_filter_disabled.title: Reverse path filtering disabled (rp_filter = 0)
rp_filter_disabled.why: Without reverse path filtering, the kernel accepts packets from source IP addresses that could not have arrived via the receiving interface — a sign of IP spoofing. This enables spoofed-source attacks and can be used to bypass firewall rules that rely on source IP.
rp_filter_disabled.how:
1. Enable immediately (takes effect now):
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1
2. Make it permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-rp-filter.conf
3. Apply all sysctl settings:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: On a public-facing server, reverse path filtering is a fundamental network hardening measure. Without it, an attacker can send packets with a forged source IP, potentially bypassing IP-based access controls or enabling amplification attacks. The fix is zero-cost and has no functional side effects on standard infrastructure.

desktop.why: On a desktop, reverse path filtering provides defence-in-depth. The practical risk is lower since no public inbound services are exposed, but enabling it costs nothing and eliminates a class of IP spoofing attacks on local network traffic.

container.why: In a container, sysctl network settings are controlled by the host kernel. This setting cannot be changed from within a standard container. Apply the fix on the host system.
container.how:
Apply on the host system (not inside the container):
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-rp-filter.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

redirects_enabled.title: ICMP redirects accepted (accept_redirects = 1)
redirects_enabled.why: ICMP redirect messages can instruct the kernel to change its routing tables. An attacker on the local network can send forged ICMP redirects to reroute traffic through a machine they control, enabling a routing hijack or man-in-the-middle attack.
redirects_enabled.how:
1. Disable immediately (takes effect now):
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0
2. Make it permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-redirects.conf
3. Apply all sysctl settings:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: ICMP redirects can be used by an attacker on the local network to poison a server's routing table, redirecting its traffic through a malicious gateway (MITM). On a server, accepting ICMP redirects should never be enabled — there is no legitimate use case on standard infrastructure.

desktop.why: ICMP redirect acceptance is a minor risk on a desktop, primarily relevant on untrusted networks (public Wi-Fi, corporate LANs). Disabling it is a good practice with no functional impact for typical desktop users.

container.why: ICMP redirect settings are kernel-level and controlled by the host. This finding is not actionable from within a container. Verify and fix on the host system.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-redirects.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

log_martians_disabled.title: Martian packet logging disabled (log_martians = 0)
log_martians_disabled.why: Martian packets have source addresses that are impossible given the routing table — a strong indicator of IP spoofing, forged packets, or scanning. Without logging them, early-stage reconnaissance and spoofing attacks leave no trace. Enabling this logging is low-cost and provides valuable forensic data.
log_martians_disabled.how:
1. Enable immediately:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians=1
2. Make it permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians=1' | sudo tee >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf
3. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: Logging martian packets on a server is essential for detecting IP spoofing and network reconnaissance. Without it, early-stage scanning and spoofing attacks leave no trace in logs, making incident investigation much harder.

desktop.why: Martian packet logging is a useful forensic tool but generates noise on busy home networks. It is a low-priority hardening item on a desktop — enable it if you want visibility into anomalous local network traffic.

container.why: Sysctl logging settings are host-level and not configurable from within a standard container. This finding is not actionable in a container context. Address it on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians=1
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

rp_filter_loose.title: Reverse path filtering in loose mode (rp_filter = 2)
rp_filter_loose.why: Loose mode (rp_filter=2) accepts packets as long as any route to the source exists, not necessarily via the receiving interface. This provides weaker protection than strict mode (=1) against IP spoofing and source-routing attacks. Strict mode drops packets whose reverse path does not match the interface they arrived on.
rp_filter_loose.how:
1. Switch to strict mode:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1
2. Make it permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-rp-filter.conf
3. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system
Note: strict mode may break asymmetric routing (e.g. multi-homed servers). Verify network connectivity after applying.

server.why: Loose mode (rp_filter=2) provides weaker protection than strict mode (=1) on a server. On a single-interface server, strict mode should be preferred as it rejects more spoofed packets. Loose mode is only justified on multi-homed servers with asymmetric routing.

desktop.why: On a single-interface desktop, loose mode offers little protection compared to strict mode. Strict mode (=1) is safe and recommended unless you have specific asymmetric routing requirements, which are uncommon on desktops.

container.why: Same as rp_filter_disabled — this is a host kernel setting that cannot be modified from within a standard container. Apply on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-rp-filter.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

tcp_syncookies_disabled.title: SYN flood protection disabled (tcp_syncookies = 0)
tcp_syncookies_disabled.why: Without SYN cookies, a TCP SYN flood (an attacker sending a high rate of SYN packets without completing the handshake) can exhaust the kernel's connection queue and prevent legitimate clients from connecting — a classic denial-of-service. SYN cookies let the kernel respond to the SYN without allocating queue state until the handshake completes, making this attack ineffective. Cost is negligible on normal traffic.
tcp_syncookies_disabled.how:
1. Enable immediately:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1
2. Make it permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
3. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: On a public-facing server, SYN cookies are essential — any TCP-listening service is a SYN flood target. Mass scanners and DoS scripts probe servers constantly; without SYN cookies, even a moderate flood can take a service offline. The fix has zero functional cost.

desktop.why: On a desktop behind NAT, the practical SYN flood risk is low (the router absorbs external packets). Enabling SYN cookies still costs nothing and is good defence-in-depth if the machine is ever moved to a more exposed network.

container.why: Sysctl networking settings are host-level — this cannot be set from inside a standard container. Apply on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1
   echo 'net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

accept_source_route_enabled.title: IP source routing accepted (accept_source_route = 1)
accept_source_route_enabled.why: Source routing lets the packet's sender specify the path it should take through the network. Accepting these packets enables IP spoofing and routing bypass: an attacker can forge the source IP and force replies back through a path they control, evading firewall rules that filter on source address. There is virtually no legitimate use for source-routed packets on modern networks.
accept_source_route_enabled.how:
1. Disable immediately (IPv4):
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route=0
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route=0
2. Disable for IPv6 too:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route=0
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route=0
3. Make permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
   echo 'net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
4. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: On a server, accepting source-routed packets allows attackers to bypass IP-based access controls and forge replies to spoofed sources. Standard infrastructure never needs source routing — disabling it has no functional impact and closes a long-known IP spoofing vector.

desktop.why: On a desktop, source routing risks are reduced by NAT but still relevant on untrusted networks (public Wi-Fi, hotel LANs). Disabling it costs nothing and is universally recommended.

container.why: Host kernel setting — not configurable from inside a standard container.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route=0
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

accept_redirects_v6_enabled.title: IPv6 ICMP redirects accepted (net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 1)
accept_redirects_v6_enabled.why: Same as the IPv4 variant: an attacker on the local network can send forged ICMPv6 redirect messages to alter the kernel's IPv6 routing table, rerouting traffic through a machine they control (man-in-the-middle / routing hijack). With IPv6 deployment increasing, this attack vector now applies to most modern systems. Hosts that are not routers have no reason to accept redirects.
accept_redirects_v6_enabled.how:
1. Disable immediately:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects=0
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects=0
2. Make permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
   echo 'net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
3. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: On a server with IPv6 enabled, accepting ICMPv6 redirects allows a local-segment attacker to poison the routing table and MITM outbound traffic. Servers are not routers — disabling redirect acceptance has no functional impact.

desktop.why: ICMPv6 redirect acceptance is risky on untrusted IPv6 networks (public Wi-Fi with IPv6, corporate guest LANs). Disabling it on a desktop is good practice and has no functional cost.

container.why: Host kernel setting — apply on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects=0
   echo 'net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

send_redirects_enabled.title: ICMP redirects sent by the host (send_redirects = 1)
send_redirects_enabled.why: Only routers should send ICMP redirects (to tell hosts about a better gateway). A non-router host that sends them gives a local-segment attacker primitive material to inject forged redirects and reroute traffic from neighbouring hosts through itself or a controlled gateway — a man-in-the-middle setup. Disabling send_redirects on non-router systems closes this vector.
send_redirects_enabled.how:
1. Disable immediately:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects=0
2. Make permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
3. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system
Note: if this machine actually is a router (multi-homed, performs IP forwarding), keep send_redirects=1 — disabling it would prevent legitimate routing optimization.

server.why: A standard server is not a router. Sending ICMP redirects from it is unnecessary and gives an attacker on the same LAN a foothold for routing manipulation. Disable unless this machine genuinely performs routing duties.

desktop.why: A desktop is never a router. Sending ICMP redirects has no use case and exposes the local network to redirect-based MITM attacks. Disable safely.

container.why: Host kernel setting — not configurable from inside a standard container.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

protected_hardlinks_disabled.title: Hardlink protection disabled (fs.protected_hardlinks = 0)
protected_hardlinks_disabled.why: Without hardlink protection, an unprivileged user can create a hardlink to any file they have read access to — including SUID binaries or files in privileged directories. This enables several local privilege escalation patterns where a vulnerability in a SUID program can be triggered against a sensitive file via a hardlink in /tmp. With protection enabled, the kernel only allows hardlinks when the user owns the source or has write access to it.
protected_hardlinks_disabled.how:
1. Enable immediately:
   sudo sysctl -w fs.protected_hardlinks=1
2. Make permanent:
   echo 'fs.protected_hardlinks=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
3. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: On a server with multiple users or any unprivileged services, hardlink protection blocks a well-known local privilege escalation pattern. Modern distros enable it by default — if it is disabled, something explicitly turned it off.

desktop.why: On a single-user desktop, the local privesc risk is lower but still real (any compromised user-space service could attempt it). Enabling has no functional cost — modern distributions set this by default.

container.why: Host kernel setting — applies to the entire system, not the container namespace. Apply on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w fs.protected_hardlinks=1
   echo 'fs.protected_hardlinks=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

protected_symlinks_disabled.title: Symlink protection disabled (fs.protected_symlinks = 0)
protected_symlinks_disabled.why: Without symlink protection, a classic TOCTOU (time-of-check-to-time-of-use) attack becomes feasible: an unprivileged user creates a symlink in a world-writable directory (typically /tmp) pointing at a sensitive file, then waits for a privileged process to follow the symlink — overwriting or reading the target with the privileged process's permissions. With protection enabled, the kernel refuses to follow symlinks in sticky-bit directories unless the symlink owner matches the directory owner or the process owner.
protected_symlinks_disabled.how:
1. Enable immediately:
   sudo sysctl -w fs.protected_symlinks=1
2. Make permanent:
   echo 'fs.protected_symlinks=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
3. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: On a server with multi-user activity or scheduled jobs running as root, symlink protection blocks the /tmp TOCTOU exploit family (a recurring source of CVEs over the past two decades). Modern distros enable it by default.

desktop.why: On a desktop, the practical risk is reduced but the /tmp symlink race remains a known attack pattern usable by any local malicious script. Enabling has no functional cost — modern distributions set this by default.

container.why: Host kernel setting — applies to the entire host filesystem, not the container namespace. Apply on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w fs.protected_symlinks=1
   echo 'fs.protected_symlinks=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

apparmor_inactive.title: AppArmor installed but the service is not running
apparmor_inactive.why: AppArmor enforces mandatory access controls — restricting what files, network sockets, and capabilities each program can use, on top of standard Unix permissions. When the service is down, every confined profile (Firefox, snap apps, cups, ntpd, sshd on many distros, etc.) runs without confinement — a compromised program can do anything its user account can do. AppArmor is one of the few defences against post-exploitation lateral movement on Debian-family systems.
apparmor_inactive.how:
1. Enable and start the service:
   sudo systemctl enable --now apparmor
2. Verify status:
   sudo aa-status
3. If startup fails, check the journal for errors:
   sudo journalctl -u apparmor -b

server.why: On a server, an inactive AppArmor strips the per-service confinement that limits what nginx, mariadb, or any other daemon can do if compromised. Re-activating it is a one-command fix with no functional cost on standard distros.

desktop.why: On a desktop, AppArmor confines untrusted apps (browsers, snaps, flatpaks) which are the most likely entry vector for malware. Re-enabling it costs nothing and meaningfully reduces blast radius after a successful exploit.

container.why: AppArmor profiles inside containers depend on the host's AppArmor service. Address this on the host system.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo systemctl enable --now apparmor
   sudo aa-status

apparmor_no_enforce.title: AppArmor active but no profile is in enforce mode
apparmor_no_enforce.why: AppArmor profiles have two modes: enforce (deny disallowed operations) and complain (log them but allow). When all profiles are in complain mode — or none are in enforce — AppArmor logs policy violations but never blocks anything. The defensive value drops to near zero: an attacker exploiting a confined process is not stopped, only observed (and only if you read the logs).
apparmor_no_enforce.how:
1. List profiles and their mode:
   sudo aa-status
2. Switch all installed profiles to enforce:
   sudo aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/*
3. Re-check that profiles loaded successfully:
   sudo aa-status
Note: review each profile first — a poorly written profile in enforce mode can break the app. Standard distro profiles for nginx, mysql, snap apps, etc. are safe to enforce. Custom profiles should be tested in complain first.

server.why: Complain-only AppArmor on a server provides telemetry but no protection. Audit each installed profile, then enforce. Most distro-provided profiles are tested and safe to enforce immediately.

desktop.why: Even on a desktop, complain-mode profiles do nothing in practice — almost no user reads AppArmor logs. Enforce the standard Firefox / snap / flatpak profiles to actually benefit from the MAC layer.

container.why: Container AppArmor profile mode is controlled by the host or the container runtime. Address on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/*
   sudo aa-status

apparmor_no_profiles.title: AppArmor active but no profiles are loaded at all
apparmor_no_profiles.why: AppArmor without profiles is just an idle kernel module — it does nothing. Common causes are a freshly installed distro that did not ship the apparmor-profiles package, or a Kali / minimal install where the policy set was omitted. Installing the standard profile pack adds dozens of confinements for common services (cups, ntpd, mysqld, snap apps, libreoffice, …) without any custom work.
apparmor_no_profiles.how:
1. Install the AppArmor profile packages:
   sudo apt install apparmor-profiles apparmor-profiles-extra
2. (Optional) install additional snap / firefox profiles:
   sudo apt install snapd-confine-profiles
3. Reload AppArmor to load them:
   sudo systemctl reload apparmor
4. Verify profiles loaded:
   sudo aa-status

server.why: An AppArmor-active server with zero profiles means daemons run with no MAC restriction. Installing the standard profile pack gives confinement for common services (nginx, mariadb, postfix, …) immediately.

desktop.why: On a desktop without profiles, browsers and snap apps run unconfined. The standard profile packages cost a few MB and confine the most likely attack vectors.

container.why: Container AppArmor profiles are loaded by the host. Address on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo apt install apparmor-profiles apparmor-profiles-extra
   sudo systemctl reload apparmor

no_enforce.title: No active mandatory access control on the system
no_enforce.why: Neither SELinux (Red Hat / Fedora family) nor AppArmor (Debian / Ubuntu family) is enforcing — the system runs entirely on standard Unix DAC (discretionary access control). DAC alone gives every program the full power of its user account. Compromising a single daemon means the attacker can do everything the daemon's user can. MAC layers like AppArmor or SELinux apply per-program restrictions that DAC cannot express, and they are the practical defence against post-exploitation lateral movement.
no_enforce.how:
Pick the MAC layer matching your distro:
Debian / Ubuntu / Mint / Kali → enable AppArmor:
   sudo apt install apparmor apparmor-profiles apparmor-profiles-extra
   sudo systemctl enable --now apparmor
   sudo aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/*
Fedora / RHEL / CentOS / Rocky → enable SELinux:
   sudo setenforce 1
   sudo sed -i 's/SELINUX=permissive/SELINUX=enforcing/' /etc/selinux/config
   sudo systemctl reboot

server.why: A server without any MAC layer is one CVE away from full system compromise. AppArmor or SELinux is mandatory hardening for any production server.

desktop.why: Without MAC, an exploit against your browser or any user-space app inherits your full user privileges. Enabling AppArmor on Debian-family is a one-command win with no functional cost.

container.why: Container MAC depends on the host. Enable AppArmor or SELinux on the host to apply confinement to all containers.
container.how: Apply on the host system, then ensure the container runtime is allowed to apply per-container profiles (Docker, containerd, podman all support this by default once the host MAC is enabled).

no_mac.title: No MAC framework is even installed
no_mac.why: Same as 'no_enforce' but worse: not only is no MAC layer running, none is installed either. The system has only standard Unix permissions for isolation. On modern Linux this is unusual — both AppArmor and SELinux are widely packaged. The most common case is a stripped-down minimal install (Alpine, custom-built distro, container base image used as a host).
no_mac.how:
Install the appropriate framework for your distro:
Debian / Ubuntu / Mint → AppArmor:
   sudo apt install apparmor apparmor-profiles apparmor-profiles-extra
   sudo systemctl enable --now apparmor
Fedora / RHEL / CentOS → SELinux:
   sudo dnf install selinux-policy-targeted policycoreutils
   sudo setenforce 1
Reboot if SELinux is freshly enabled — relabeling at first boot may take several minutes.

server.why: A server with no MAC framework installed is operating on DAC-only isolation. Installing AppArmor or SELinux is the baseline hardening before any production deployment.

desktop.why: Most desktop distros ship AppArmor by default; finding no MAC installed at all is typically a minimal install. Add the framework + profile pack.

container.why: Container hosts without MAC offer no per-container security boundary beyond namespaces. Install AppArmor on the host as a baseline.
container.how:
Apply on the container host:
   sudo apt install apparmor apparmor-profiles
   sudo systemctl enable --now apparmor

selinux_disabled.title: SELinux is disabled at the boot level (no MAC enforcement)
selinux_disabled.why: On Red Hat family distros, SELinux disabled (not just permissive) means the kernel does not even load the policy. Every process runs without MAC restrictions — services that are normally tightly confined (httpd, sshd, mariadb) run as if SELinux did not exist. A compromised service can read any file its user can read, write anywhere the user can write, and connect to any network endpoint. Re-enabling SELinux on a long-disabled system requires a filesystem relabel and reboot.
selinux_disabled.how:
1. Edit /etc/selinux/config and change:
   SELINUX=disabled
   to:
   SELINUX=enforcing
   (or SELINUX=permissive first for a transition period — see note below)
2. Force a filesystem relabel on next boot:
   sudo touch /.autorelabel
3. Reboot:
   sudo systemctl reboot
Note: if SELinux has been disabled for a long time, set SELINUX=permissive first and run with permissive for a few days to surface and fix any custom-app policy issues, then switch to enforcing once the audit log is clean.

server.why: On a Red Hat-family server, SELinux is the dominant MAC layer and a Selinux-disabled server loses years of per-service confinement work (httpd_t, mysqld_t, ssh_t, etc.). Re-enabling is a mandatory step in any production hardening pass.

desktop.why: SELinux on a desktop confines services (cups, NetworkManager, …) that are common attack targets. Re-enabling costs the relabel time but provides meaningful protection.

container.why: SELinux on the host applies container labels (svirt_*) that isolate containers from each other and from the host. Re-enabling on the host re-enables this layer.
container.how: Apply on the host system following the same procedure as on a bare-metal host (edit /etc/selinux/config, touch /.autorelabel, reboot).

iptables_bypass.title: Docker is set to write its own iptables rules (`iptables=true`), bypassing UFW
iptables_bypass.why: Docker's default behaviour is to insert its own ACCEPT rules into the DOCKER and DOCKER-USER chains, evaluated BEFORE UFW's chains. Any container `-p` flag exposes its port directly to the world — UFW deny rules for that port silently do nothing.
