Operators routinely discover this only when a production database or admin panel is reachable from the public internet despite UFW reporting it as blocked. The mitigation is to either set Docker's `iptables=false` in /etc/docker/daemon.json (and accept that Docker port exposure is now manual) or to bind containers explicitly to 127.0.0.1 / a private interface.
iptables_bypass.how:
Pick one approach:
Option A — keep Docker's iptables management but bind containers to localhost or a specific interface:
   docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 my-app
   # or via docker-compose:
   ports:
     - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
Option B — disable Docker's iptables management entirely and write the rules yourself:
   sudo nano /etc/docker/daemon.json
   {"iptables": false}
   sudo systemctl restart docker
   # NOTE: containers will no longer have outbound network until you add NAT rules manually.
Option C — leave Docker's iptables management on but add explicit UFW rules in the DOCKER-USER chain (more advanced, see Docker docs).

server.why: On a server, this is one of the most common Docker security incidents — a container intended to be LAN-only ends up internet-exposed. Audit every `docker run -p` or `ports:` declaration and bind to a specific interface (127.0.0.1 or a private IP) unless the container is explicitly meant to be public.

desktop.why: On a desktop behind NAT, the external risk is moderated but local-network exposure is real (your container is reachable from any other device on the Wi-Fi). Bind to 127.0.0.1 for development services.

container.why: This finding is about the Docker daemon's configuration, which lives on the host. Address on the host.

exposed_port.title: Docker container exposes a port (UFW is bypassed; still LAN-reachable)
exposed_port.why: The container is publishing a port via `-p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT` or a `ports:` declaration. Because Docker manages iptables (see docker.iptables_bypass), this port is reachable from at least the LAN and possibly the public internet depending on the publish address (default 0.0.0.0 = all interfaces). UFW deny rules for this port have no effect. Whether this is a problem depends on what the container offers: a self-hosted dashboard, a database admin UI, or a redis with no auth are all classic Docker exposure incidents.
exposed_port.how:
1. Audit what the container exposes:
   docker ps
   docker inspect <container> | jq '.[0].NetworkSettings.Ports'
2. If the service is internal-only, restrict the publish address:
   docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 ...   # localhost only
   docker run -p 192.168.1.10:8080:8080 ... # specific LAN IP only
3. If the container must be reachable but only from specific clients, add an iptables rule in the DOCKER-USER chain:
   sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER -s <trusted-ip> -j ACCEPT
   sudo iptables -A DOCKER-USER -j DROP

server.why: On a server, every exposed Docker port is potentially internet-facing. Treat each `-p` declaration as a public-port decision, not a local-port decision.

desktop.why: On a desktop, exposed ports are reachable from other devices on the same LAN — fine for development with trusted devices, risky on shared Wi-Fi.

container.why: Port exposure is configured at container-launch time on the host. Address there.

exposed_bypass_ufw.title: Docker container port is exposed AND Docker iptables management is bypassing UFW
exposed_bypass_ufw.why: Two issues combined: the container is publishing a port (`-p`) and Docker is configured to write iptables rules that bypass UFW. The result is that the port is fully reachable on whatever publish address was specified (default 0.0.0.0 = every interface, including the public one), with UFW totally unable to block it. This is the worst-case Docker exposure pattern — visible in the wild every time a developer ships a 'just for testing' container to a public-IP VPS. CVEs in the exposed application are now public-facing.
exposed_bypass_ufw.how:
Two simultaneous fixes needed:
1. Restrict the publish address of the offending container:
   - Stop and recreate the container with -p 127.0.0.1:HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT
   - Or edit docker-compose.yml: 'ports: ["127.0.0.1:HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT"]'
2. Decide on the Docker / UFW integration (see docker.iptables_bypass for the long form):
   - Bind explicitly (simpler): keep iptables=true, always specify the publish address
   - Or disable Docker's iptables (advanced): /etc/docker/daemon.json {"iptables": false}
3. Re-verify with:
   sudo iptables -L DOCKER-USER -n
   ss -tlnp | grep <port>

server.why: On a public-facing server, this combination means a container is internet-exposed despite UFW saying otherwise. Fix immediately — rotate any credentials that may have been exposed.

desktop.why: Even behind NAT, this combination exposes the container to the entire local network including untrusted devices on shared Wi-Fi. The fix is the same as on a server.

container.why: Port exposure and Docker daemon config are host-level. Address on the host.

open_local.title: Service port reachable from the LAN (UFW rule allows the local subnet)
open_local.why: The UFW rule for this port permits traffic from the local network (e.g. `ALLOW from 192.168.1.0/24`). The service is therefore reachable from any device on that subnet — fine when the LAN is fully trusted (home office, corporate VLAN), risky on shared Wi-Fi where untrusted devices coexist (public Wi-Fi, conferences, hotel rooms). The finding is informational on a trusted LAN and a real concern on an untrusted one.
open_local.how:
Decide based on the network this machine sits on:
1. Trusted LAN (home, corp VLAN) → keep the rule; the finding is informational.
2. Untrusted LAN (shared Wi-Fi, IoT segment) → tighten the rule:
   sudo ufw delete allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port <port>
   sudo ufw allow from <trusted-ip> to any port <port>
3. Internal-only service that should never face any external client → bind the daemon to 127.0.0.1 instead of relying on firewall:
   # in daemon config (sshd_config, postgresql.conf, redis.conf, …):
   bind 127.0.0.1
   listen_addresses = 'localhost'

server.why: On a server, an open-local port that exposes admin tooling (database UIs, monitoring dashboards, ssh) deserves an explicit decision — is the LAN actually trustworthy? Restrict to specific IPs when possible.

desktop.why: On a desktop, the LAN trust level changes constantly (home / coffee shop / hotel). Consider binding services to 127.0.0.1 instead of relying on the LAN whitelist.

container.why: Container port exposure is host-level. Adjust UFW on the host or restrict the container's publish address.

active_disabled.title: Service is running now but not enabled to start at boot
active_disabled.why: The service is active in the current session but its systemd unit is not enabled, so a reboot stops it for good. Operators commonly run into this after troubleshooting (`systemctl start` works, the issue disappears, the operator forgets the `systemctl enable`). The next maintenance reboot — possibly unattended, possibly during an outage — silently drops the service. Whether this matters depends on what the service does; for critical security services (fail2ban, auditd, clamav, apparmor) it is a real risk.
active_disabled.how:
1. Confirm the service is actually what you want at boot:
   sudo systemctl is-active <service>
   sudo systemctl is-enabled <service>
2. Enable persistence:
   sudo systemctl enable <service>
3. Verify on next reboot or via systemd-analyze:
   sudo systemd-analyze verify <service>.service

server.why: On a server, services not enabled at boot survive only until the next reboot — which on a production server is the wrong time to discover that fail2ban or auditd is gone.

desktop.why: On a desktop, reboots are more frequent (laptop sleep cycles, kernel updates). A security service that is active now but not enabled is gone after the next shutdown.

container.why: Containers typically do not use systemd boot enablement (they launch a single command). This finding applies to host-level services — address there.

installed_inactive_critical.title: A high-criticality service is installed but neither active nor enabled
installed_inactive_critical.why: Packages providing high-impact protection (fail2ban, auditd, clamav, apparmor, rkhunter, …) are installed on the system but are not running and will not start at boot. They consume disk space without providing any defence — the package is present but the service is dormant. The most common cause is an aborted install / first-run failure where the systemd unit was masked or disabled and never re-enabled. The defensive value of the package is zero in this state.
installed_inactive_critical.how:
1. Check why the service is inactive (the journal usually says why it failed to start):
   sudo systemctl status <service>
   sudo journalctl -u <service> -b
2. If the unit is masked, unmask it first:
   sudo systemctl unmask <service>
3. Enable and start:
   sudo systemctl enable --now <service>
4. Re-verify:
   sudo systemctl status <service>
Note: if the service won't start (config error, missing data file, port already used), fix the underlying issue — leaving it disabled silently is worse than uninstalling.

server.why: On a server, an installed but dormant security tool is misleading documentation — it suggests the protection exists when it does not. Either fix the activation or uninstall the package and document the choice explicitly.

desktop.why: On a desktop, a dormant clamav or apparmor offers no protection. Re-activate, or uninstall if you decided not to use it (and remember why).

container.why: Containers usually do not run multiple long-lived services. If a security tool is installed but inactive inside a container, either run it as a sidecar/init or remove the package.

db_outdated.title: rkhunter signature database is outdated (no recent rkhunter --update)
db_outdated.why: rkhunter detects known rootkits by matching binaries, file properties and process patterns against a signature database. The database needs to be refreshed regularly — the rootkit landscape evolves and new patterns are published. An outdated database means newly identified rootkits go undetected and the tool produces a false sense of security: the scan reports 'clean' because it doesn't know what to look for.
db_outdated.how:
1. Refresh the database now:
   sudo rkhunter --update
2. Re-run a scan to confirm the database is fresh:
   sudo rkhunter --check --skip-keypress
3. Automate updates via cron (daily is fine):
   echo '0 4 * * * root rkhunter --update --quiet' | sudo tee /etc/cron.d/rkhunter-update

server.why: On a server, a stale rootkit database is one of the silent-failure modes — the tool keeps reporting clean while missing recent threats. Add the cron job once and forget about it.

desktop.why: Desktop reboots and sleep cycles often interrupt scheduled updates. A weekly cron is enough; verify the database date occasionally with `rkhunter --versioncheck`.

container.why: rkhunter is typically run on the host, not inside individual containers. Address on the host.

no_scan.title: rkhunter is installed but no completed scan was found in the logs
no_scan.why: rkhunter only detects rootkits when it actually runs. An installed-but-never-executed rkhunter provides zero protection: no scan has compared the current system state against the signature database. The most common cause is install + first-run-failure where the user installed the package but the initial scan crashed (missing /var/log/rkhunter directory, permission error, custom config rejected). A second common case is package installed by a meta-package without scheduled runs (no cron entry).
no_scan.how:
1. Run a scan now to verify rkhunter works on this system:
   sudo rkhunter --check --skip-keypress
2. If the scan succeeds, the log under /var/log/rkhunter.log proves it ran.
3. Schedule daily scans via cron:
   echo '30 4 * * * root rkhunter --check --skip-keypress --quiet --rwo' | sudo tee /etc/cron.d/rkhunter-scan
4. (Optional) configure email alerts on findings — edit /etc/rkhunter.conf and set MAIL-ON-WARNING.

server.why: On a server, an idle rkhunter is misleading documentation — it looks installed but produces no findings ever. Schedule the daily scan.

desktop.why: On a desktop, weekly scans are usually enough; daily is fine if you don't mind the extra log noise.

container.why: rkhunter runs on the host. Schedule on the host.

scan_old.title: Last rkhunter scan is too old to be meaningful
scan_old.why: rkhunter is installed and has run in the past, but the last scan is older than the freshness threshold (typically 30 days). The system has had a full month-worth of changes (package updates, kernel upgrades, new applications) that the last rkhunter scan never saw. Detection coverage degrades quickly when the gap between scans grows — newly installed binaries cannot be compared to a baseline that pre-dates them.
scan_old.how:
1. Run a fresh scan immediately:
   sudo rkhunter --check --skip-keypress
2. If a cron entry exists but is not firing, check for errors:
   sudo journalctl -t cron --since '7 days ago' | grep rkhunter
3. Re-schedule via /etc/cron.d/rkhunter-scan (see rootkit.no_scan for the cron line).

server.why: On a server, a months-old rkhunter scan provides no current visibility. Reschedule and verify the cron is actually firing (the most common reason for stale scans is a broken cron entry, not a missing one).

desktop.why: On a desktop, lapses are normal (laptop off for weeks, etc.). Run a fresh scan after a long offline period before trusting the previous result.

container.why: rkhunter on the host monitors the host filesystem. Schedule on the host.

uncovered.title: Listening port has no UFW rule and the default policy allows it through
uncovered.why: A service is bound to a network interface and accepting connections on a specific port, but UFW has neither an explicit ALLOW nor an explicit DENY rule for that port. Whether the port is reachable depends entirely on the UFW default-incoming policy: when it is ALLOW, the port is wide open; when it is DENY, the default deny catches it. The finding fires when the default does not catch the port — meaning the service is reachable without anyone having explicitly decided it should be.
uncovered.how:
Two possible actions depending on intent:
1. The port SHOULD be reachable (it is a legitimate service) → add an explicit ALLOW rule with the smallest acceptable source scope:
   sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port <port>
2. The port should NOT be reachable (the service is internal-only) → either bind the daemon to 127.0.0.1 (best) or add an explicit DENY:
   sudo ufw deny <port>
3. Re-verify:
   sudo ufw status verbose
   ss -tlnp | grep ':<port>'

server.why: On a server, every unmatched listening port is effectively undocumented. Make the decision explicit: ALLOW from specific clients, or DENY, or bind to localhost.

desktop.why: On a desktop, unmatched listening ports often come from local development services (an IDE on 5173, a node app on 3000). They should typically bind to 127.0.0.1.

container.why: Container port exposure goes through the host UFW. Address there or restrict the container's publish address.

uncovered_netbios.title: NetBIOS / Samba ports are listening without LAN-only UFW restriction
uncovered_netbios.why: Ports 137/udp (NetBIOS Name Service), 138/udp (NetBIOS Datagram), 139/tcp (NetBIOS Session) and 445/tcp (SMB) are foundational Windows file-sharing protocols. They should ONLY be reachable from a trusted LAN — never from the public internet, never from untrusted neighbours. SMB over an open network is the WannaCry / EternalBlue attack surface. UFW has no explicit LAN-only rule for these ports today, so they may be reachable beyond their intended scope.
uncovered_netbios.how:
1. Restrict the ports to your LAN subnet:
   sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 137 proto udp
   sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 138 proto udp
   sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 139 proto tcp
   sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 445 proto tcp
2. Re-verify Samba binds correctly:
   ss -tlnp | grep -E ':(139|445)\b'
3. (Recommended) tighten smb.conf 'hosts allow' to match the LAN subnet too — defence in depth.

server.why: On a server providing SMB, the rule must restrict to clients that should actually mount shares. Allowing 0.0.0.0 means any internet host can attempt SMB auth — a high-noise / high-risk surface.

desktop.why: Desktop Samba (folder shared with home network) belongs strictly on the LAN. Restrict to the subnet you use at home.

container.why: Containerised Samba publishes its ports through the host. Restrict at the UFW level on the host.

not_enabled.title: NTP synchronisation is not enabled (no time source configured)
not_enabled.why: Without NTP, the system clock drifts at the hardware oscillator's rate — typically tens of seconds per day, sometimes more. The cascading consequences are bigger than they look: TLS certificate validation fails when the clock skew exceeds a few minutes, Kerberos tickets stop being accepted, log timestamps no longer line up with reality (forensics gets harder), scheduled jobs fire at the wrong time, and distributed systems lose consensus. NTP is one of the cheapest baseline configurations on a Linux system.
not_enabled.how:
On systemd-based distros (Debian/Ubuntu/Fedora — the common case):
1. Enable and start systemd-timesyncd:
   sudo systemctl enable --now systemd-timesyncd
2. Verify it picked up a time source:
   timedatectl status
   timedatectl show-timesync
Alternative — full chrony (more accurate, often preferred on servers):
   sudo apt install chrony
   sudo systemctl enable --now chrony
   chronyc tracking

server.why: On a server, clock drift breaks TLS, certificates, scheduled jobs and distributed-system coordination. Enabling NTP is non-negotiable for production.

desktop.why: Most desktop distros enable NTP by default; this finding usually means a deliberate disable or a chrony/timesyncd conflict. Verify and re-enable.

container.why: Containers normally inherit the host's clock. The finding usually means the HOST has no NTP configured — fix on the host.

not_synchronized.title: NTP service is running but the clock is not synchronised to a source
not_synchronized.why: systemd-timesyncd / chronyd is active but it has not (yet) locked on to a usable time source. Causes include: outbound UDP/123 blocked by a firewall (typical on hardened networks), no internet access on the host, an empty or wrong-configured ntp.conf / timesyncd.conf, or all configured servers are unreachable. The service appears healthy in `systemctl status` but the clock is not actually being adjusted — drift continues.
not_synchronized.how:
1. Check what the service is trying:
   timedatectl status
   timedatectl show-timesync
   # or for chrony:
   chronyc sources
   chronyc tracking
2. Verify outbound UDP/123 is allowed (the most common silent failure):
   sudo ufw status | grep 123
3. Replace the default pool with a server you control or pool.ntp.org explicitly:
   sudo nano /etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf
   [Time]
   NTP=pool.ntp.org
   sudo systemctl restart systemd-timesyncd
4. Re-check after a couple of minutes:
   timedatectl status

server.why: On a server, an unsynchronised NTP service is worse than no NTP because the documentation lies — the service is 'running' but the clock is not converging. Fix the network or configuration issue.

desktop.why: On a desktop, the cause is often captive-portal Wi-Fi blocking NTP, or a corporate firewall. Either accept the drift (desktop, ephemeral) or use the corporate NTP server.

container.why: Container clock comes from the host. Fix host NTP first; container clocks will follow automatically.

no_jails.title: fail2ban is running but no jails are configured (no protection actually active)
no_jails.why: fail2ban's defensive value comes from its jails — each jail watches a specific log (sshd, postfix, nginx) and bans IPs that hit a fail threshold. A fail2ban daemon with no jails enabled is the equivalent of a security camera that records nothing: the service is 'running' but it monitors nothing and bans nobody. The most common cause is a default config where every jail is `enabled = false` and the operator never re-enabled the one that matters (typically sshd).
no_jails.how:
1. Enable the sshd jail (the baseline for SSH protection):
   sudo nano /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
   [sshd]
   enabled = true
2. Restart fail2ban so the jail is picked up:
   sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
3. Verify the jail is active:
   sudo fail2ban-client status
   sudo fail2ban-client status sshd

server.why: On a server, the SSH brute-force surface is constant — bots scan every public IP looking for weak ssh credentials. fail2ban-with-no-jails offers zero protection against this. The sshd jail must be enabled.

desktop.why: On a desktop with SSH not exposed to the internet, fail2ban is less critical. Either enable the sshd jail anyway as defence-in-depth, or uninstall fail2ban if you don't expose SSH.

container.why: fail2ban is typically run on the host that owns the SSH endpoint, not inside containers. Enable on the host.

service_inactive.title: fail2ban is installed but the service is not running
service_inactive.why: Without the daemon, no log is being watched, no IP is being banned, and the protection promised by fail2ban does not exist. The package is installed but inert. Common causes are a startup failure (typically a malformed jail.local — fail2ban refuses to start on syntax errors), the service being masked, or a deliberate stop during a maintenance session that was never reversed.
service_inactive.how:
1. Check why the service is inactive:
   sudo systemctl status fail2ban
   sudo journalctl -u fail2ban -b
2. If a config error is reported, fix it:
   sudo fail2ban-client -t   # config syntax check
3. Unmask if necessary then start:
   sudo systemctl unmask fail2ban
   sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
4. Verify:
   sudo fail2ban-client status

server.why: A server with fail2ban installed but inactive has the worst of both worlds: documentation claims protection that does not exist. Either start the service or uninstall and document the choice.

desktop.why: Same as server — installed but inactive is misleading. Decide: start it, or uninstall.

container.why: fail2ban watches host logs and manages host iptables. Address on the host.

found.title: A DDNS client is installed — your IP may be published to a public DNS name
found.why: Dynamic DNS clients (ddclient, no-ip, inadyn, …) periodically publish your current public IP to a hostname under a provider (yourdomain.no-ip.org, mydevice.duckdns.org, …). The hostname is then resolvable from anywhere on the internet — anyone who knows it can reach your public IP, even if it changes. DDNS itself is not a vulnerability, but it turns 'IP exposure' into 'persistent name exposure'. Every service you publish becomes effectively internet-targeted once the DDNS name is known to a scanner.
found.how:
Decide whether DDNS is intentional:
1. Intentional (remote access to home services, off-site backup target, etc.) → audit every port that is reachable on the public IP:
   sudo ufw status
   ss -tlnp
   Treat your DDNS name as a public asset and harden every exposed service accordingly.
2. Unintentional or leftover (e.g. from a previous router or test setup) → disable the client:
   sudo systemctl disable --now ddclient   # or whichever client is running
   sudo apt remove --purge ddclient

server.why: On a server intentionally exposing services to the internet, DDNS is a design choice — but every port behind it must be hardened as if it were on a static public IP. Document which ports are intentionally exposed and harden them explicitly.

desktop.why: On a desktop, DDNS is usually a remnant of remote-access experiments or a deprecated VPN setup. Confirm it is wanted; if not, disable and remove the client.

container.why: DDNS clients usually run on the host, not in containers. Address on the host.

warn.title: DDNS detected and exposes one or more ports to the public internet
warn.why: The DDNS client is publishing your public IP under a name AND one or more open ports are reachable on that IP. Anyone who resolves the DDNS name reaches those services — bots routinely enumerate DDNS providers looking for exposed admin panels, SMB shares, RDP, ssh with default credentials, Plex servers with no auth, etc. The combination of DDNS + open port is one of the most common 'how did I get hacked' patterns on residential connections.
warn.how:
1. List exposed ports the DDNS name points at:
   sudo ufw status
   ss -tlnp
2. For each port:
   - Is it intended to be public? → harden the service (strong creds, TLS, rate limiting, IP whitelist when feasible).
   - Is it accidental? → close it:
     sudo ufw deny <port>
     # or unbind the service from the public interface
3. Re-test from outside the network:
   curl -v http://<your-ddns-name>:<port>

server.why: On a server, every DDNS-reachable port is a public service. Inventory them, harden them, and remove anything not explicitly intended.

desktop.why: On a desktop, this finding is usually the cause of a real incident — a home device became reachable from the internet. Close anything you don't need.

container.why: Container ports published via the host become reachable through DDNS too. Close at the host UFW level or unpublish from the container.

risky_fs.title: Risky filesystem kernel modules loaded
risky_fs.why: Filesystem drivers (cramfs, freevxfs, hfs, hfsplus, jffs2, squashfs, udf, usb_storage) expand kernel attack surface unnecessarily on servers. Vulnerabilities in these drivers can be triggered by mounting a maliciously crafted filesystem image or inserting a USB device, potentially enabling privilege escalation or arbitrary code execution in kernel space.
risky_fs.how:
1. Unload the module now:
   sudo modprobe -r <module_name>
2. Blacklist to prevent reloading:
   echo 'blacklist <module>' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-fs.conf
   echo 'install <module> /bin/false' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-fs.conf
3. Rebuild initramfs:
   sudo update-initramfs -u
Note: only blacklist modules your system does not use (e.g. usb_storage is needed for USB drives).

server.why: Exotic filesystem modules (cramfs, freevxfs, hfs, hfsplus, jffs2, squashfs, udf) expand kernel attack surface on a server. Vulnerabilities in these drivers can be triggered by a crafted filesystem image, potentially enabling kernel-space privilege escalation. Blacklist what you do not use.

desktop.why: Most of these filesystems are not needed on a typical desktop. However, if you mount removable media with unusual filesystems (e.g. HFS+ from a Mac drive, UDF from a DVD), blacklisting those specific modules would prevent mounting them. Evaluate which ones you actually need before blacklisting.

container.why: Kernel module loading is restricted by default in containers (CAP_SYS_MODULE not granted). This finding is not actionable from within a container — address it on the host system.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   echo 'blacklist <module>' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-fs.conf
   echo 'install <module> /bin/false' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-fs.conf
   sudo update-initramfs -u

risky_net.title: Risky network protocol kernel modules loaded
risky_net.why: Protocols like DCCP, SCTP, RDS, and TIPC have had critical kernel vulnerabilities (CVEs with remote code execution and privilege escalation). These protocols are rarely needed on standard servers and represent unnecessary kernel attack surface. Loading them makes the system exploitable by sending crafted network packets to any open socket.
risky_net.how:
1. Unload the module now:
   sudo modprobe -r <module_name>
2. Blacklist to prevent reloading:
   echo 'blacklist <module>' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-net.conf
   echo 'install <module> /bin/false' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-net.conf
3. Rebuild initramfs:
   sudo update-initramfs -u
Note: SCTP is used by some telephony and clustering software. Verify before blacklisting.

server.why: Protocols DCCP, SCTP, RDS, and TIPC have had critical kernel CVEs with remote code execution and privilege escalation. These protocols are essentially never used on standard servers. Their presence in the running kernel means a crafted network packet could trigger a known kernel vulnerability.

desktop.why: These network protocols are almost never used on a desktop. Blacklisting them has no practical impact on desktop networking and closes a class of historical kernel vulnerabilities.

container.why: Kernel module loading is restricted in containers. This finding is not actionable from within a container — address it on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   echo 'blacklist <module>' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-net.conf
   echo 'install <module> /bin/false' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-net.conf
   sudo update-initramfs -u

ufw_disabled_listeners_present.title: Services listening on IPv6 but UFW IPv6 support is disabled
ufw_disabled_listeners_present.why: With UFW IPv6 disabled (IPV6=no in /etc/default/ufw), no ip6tables rules are loaded. Any service listening on a dual-stack address (::) is reachable from the network over IPv6 without any firewall filtering, regardless of what UFW shows for IPv4.
ufw_disabled_listeners_present.how:
1. Enable UFW IPv6 support:
   sudo nano /etc/default/ufw  →  IPV6=yes
2. Reload UFW to apply ip6tables rules:
   sudo ufw reload
3. Verify ip6tables rules are now active:
   sudo ip6tables -L INPUT -n | head -20

server.why: If UFW IPv6 support is disabled (IPV6=no) but services listen on IPv6 addresses, those ports are completely unmanaged by UFW. All IPv6 inbound traffic reaches the service without any filtering. On a server, this is a significant firewall gap that must be corrected.

desktop.why: On a desktop, this finding is informational. Most services listening on IPv6 are bound to loopback (::1) or link-local addresses (fe80::) with no external reachability. Enable UFW IPv6 support as best practice, but the immediate risk is low.

container.why: IPv6 management in containers is handled by the host network stack. This finding is typically not actionable from within a container. Check the host UFW configuration.

port_no_v6_rule.title: Service listening on IPv6 without a UFW IPv6 rule
port_no_v6_rule.why: A service bound to an IPv6 address with no corresponding UFW rule relies only on the default policy. If the default policy is permissive or unset, the service is reachable from any IPv6 source with no filtering. Firewall policies should be explicit for all listening addresses.
port_no_v6_rule.how:
1. Identify which service is listening:
   sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':::'
2. Add an explicit UFW rule (applies to both IPv4 and IPv6 by default):
   sudo ufw allow <port>/tcp
3. Or deny it explicitly if the service should not be reachable:
   sudo ufw deny <port>/tcp
4. Reload:
   sudo ufw reload

server.why: A service listening on IPv6 without an explicit UFW rule is accessible via IPv6 but unfiltered. On a server with a public IPv6 address, this creates an uncontrolled exposure path that bypasses all your IPv4 firewall rules. Add explicit rules for every listening port.

desktop.why: On a desktop, most IPv6 exposure is local. The risk depends on whether you have a public routable IPv6 address (a /64 from your ISP). On typical home networks using NAT or link-local only, this is informational — but adding explicit UFW rules is still good practice.

container.why: IPv6 connectivity in containers depends on the host network configuration and container runtime. If containers are not externally reachable via IPv6, this finding is informational. Check your container network setup before adding rules.

ufw_enabled_kernel_disabled.title: UFW IPv6 enabled but kernel IPv6 support is disabled
ufw_enabled_kernel_disabled.why: If UFW is configured to manage IPv6 (IPV6=yes) but the kernel has IPv6 disabled (net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=1), the intended ip6tables rules are silently never loaded. The system has an inconsistent configuration that may give a false sense of IPv6 protection.
ufw_enabled_kernel_disabled.how:
1. Option A — enable IPv6 in the kernel:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=0
   echo 'net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv6.conf
   sudo sysctl --system
2. Option B — disable UFW IPv6 to match the kernel setting:
   sudo nano /etc/default/ufw  →  IPV6=no
   sudo ufw reload

no_quality_module.title: No password quality module configured (pam_pwquality / pam_cracklib)
no_quality_module.why: Without a PAM quality module, the system imposes no complexity requirements on local passwords. Users can set trivially guessable passwords (dictionary words, 'password123', single characters) that are trivial to crack offline if /etc/shadow is ever leaked.
no_quality_module.how:
1. Install pam_pwquality:
   sudo apt install libpam-pwquality
2. Configure minimum requirements in /etc/security/pwquality.conf:
   minlen = 12
   dcredit = -1
   ucredit = -1
   lcredit = -1
   ocredit = -1
3. Verify PAM includes pwquality:
   grep pam_pwquality /etc/pam.d/common-password

weak_minlen.title: Minimum password length too short (< 8 characters)
weak_minlen.why: Short passwords dramatically reduce the search space for offline brute-force and dictionary attacks. A 6-character password with common character sets can be fully cracked in minutes with modern hardware. NIST SP 800-63B recommends at least 8 characters; CIS recommends 14.
weak_minlen.how:
1. Increase minlen in /etc/security/pwquality.conf:
   sudo nano /etc/security/pwquality.conf  →  minlen = 12
2. Test the policy interactively:
   pwscore
3. Existing passwords are not affected — enforce a reset cycle for active accounts if compliance requires it

no_expiry.title: No password expiry policy configured
no_expiry.why: Without password expiry, compromised credentials remain valid indefinitely. If an attacker silently obtains a password (phishing, database leak, keylogger), they retain access until the user voluntarily changes it. Expiry forces periodic rotation and limits the exposure window.
no_expiry.how:
1. Set a global expiry policy in /etc/login.defs:
   PASS_MAX_DAYS 90
   PASS_MIN_DAYS 1
   PASS_WARN_AGE 14
2. Apply to existing accounts:
   sudo chage -M 90 <username>
3. Check current settings:
   sudo chage -l <username>
Note: NIST SP 800-63B now recommends long complex passwords without forced expiry. Adjust policy to your compliance requirements.

uid_zero.title: Non-root account with UID 0 detected
uid_zero.why: UID 0 is the superuser identifier. Any account with UID 0 has unrestricted root-equivalent access to the entire system — bypassing file permissions, sudo rules, and audit trails. A second UID-0 account is a common backdoor left by attackers or misconfigured systems. Only 'root' itself should ever hold UID 0.
uid_zero.how:
1. List all UID 0 accounts:
   awk -F: '($3 == 0) {print $1}' /etc/passwd
2. Lock or delete any non-root UID 0 account:
   sudo passwd -l <username>   # lock (preferred)
   sudo userdel <username>     # delete if no longer needed
3. Verify only root remains:
   awk -F: '($3 == 0) {print $1}' /etc/passwd  →  root

empty_password.title: Account with empty (blank) password detected
empty_password.why: An account without a password can be logged into by anyone without credentials — locally, over SSH (if PermitEmptyPasswords is on), or via su. Even with SSH key-only authentication, a single misconfiguration can open unauthenticated access. Empty passwords are never intentional in production.
empty_password.how:
1. List accounts with empty passwords:
   sudo awk -F: '($2 == "") {print $1}' /etc/shadow
2. Set a strong password immediately:
   sudo passwd <username>
3. If the account is a service account that should not be logged in:
   sudo passwd -l <username>   # lock it
4. Check SSH config: ensure PermitEmptyPasswords no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config

expired_account.title: User account with expired password detected
expired_account.why: Expired accounts may still be usable depending on PAM configuration and the value of INACTIVE in /etc/shadow. More importantly, they indicate accounts that are not actively maintained — forgotten accounts accumulate over time and represent a persistent attack surface if credentials are ever leaked.
expired_account.how:
1. List expired accounts:
   sudo chage -l <username>  →  check 'Password expired'
2. Renew the password if the account is active:
   sudo passwd <username>
3. Lock the account if it is no longer in use:
   sudo passwd -l <username>  # or: sudo usermod -e 1 <username>
4. Audit all accounts regularly:
   sudo chage --list <username> for each login user

no_shadow.title: /etc/shadow not readable — account security checks incomplete
no_shadow.why: /etc/shadow stores hashed passwords and account aging data. Without read access, bob cannot verify empty passwords, expiry policies, or UID 0 anomalies. This finding is informational only and means the audit is running without full privilege for account checks.
no_shadow.how:
1. This is not a configuration problem — run the full audit as root:
   sudo bob
2. Ensure /etc/shadow has correct permissions (640, root:shadow):
   sudo chmod 640 /etc/shadow
   sudo chown root:shadow /etc/shadow

smart_failed.title: SMART overall health check FAILED
smart_failed.why: A SMART health failure means the drive's own firmware predicts imminent failure. Data loss is likely imminent. This is the most critical disk warning — the drive should be considered unreliable immediately and replaced.
smart_failed.how:
1. Back up all data immediately — do not wait
2. Get the full SMART report:
   sudo smartctl -a <device>
3. Run a short self-test to confirm:
   sudo smartctl -t short <device>
   sudo smartctl -l selftest <device>  # after ~2 min
4. Replace the drive
5. Restore from backup to the replacement drive

reallocated_sectors.title: Reallocated sectors detected (SMART attribute 5)
reallocated_sectors.why: Reallocated sectors mean the drive has found areas that could not be written reliably and remapped them to spare sectors. A growing count indicates progressive failure — the drive is actively hiding bad areas and more may fail without warning.
reallocated_sectors.how:
1. Get the full SMART report to see the count and trend:
   sudo smartctl -a <device>
2. Run a long self-test:
   sudo smartctl -t long <device>
3. Monitor: if the count is growing over weeks, replace the drive
4. Ensure backups are current

pending_sectors.title: Current pending sectors detected (SMART attribute 197)
pending_sectors.why: Pending sectors are areas the drive has flagged for reallocation but has not yet remapped. They may already be unreadable. This is an active data-loss risk — files stored on these sectors may be unrecoverable.
pending_sectors.how:
1. Back up immediately — files on pending sectors may already be corrupt
2. Check full SMART data:
   sudo smartctl -a <device>
3. Run a filesystem check after unmounting to attempt repair:
   sudo fsck -f <device>
4. If the count persists or grows, replace the drive

uncorrectable_errors.title: Offline uncorrectable errors detected (SMART attribute 198)
uncorrectable_errors.why: Uncorrectable errors are sectors that could not be read even with multiple retries. Data in these sectors is permanently lost. Unlike pending sectors, these have already failed — there is no recovery without a prior backup.
uncorrectable_errors.how:
1. Back up immediately — data in affected sectors is permanently gone
2. Check the full SMART report:
   sudo smartctl -a <device>
3. Run a filesystem check:
   sudo fsck -f <device>  # when unmounted
4. Replace the drive — uncorrectable errors indicate physical media damage

partition_critical.title: Partition is critically full (≥ 90%)
partition_critical.why: A full partition causes service failures: databases crash, web servers return 500 errors, logs stop being written (masking security incidents), and processes needing temporary files fail unpredictably. At 100%, the system may become unresponsive.
partition_critical.how:
1. Find what is consuming space:
   du -sh <mountpoint>/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20
2. Common culprits:
   - Logs: sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M
   - Old kernels: sudo apt autoremove
   - Docker: docker system prune
3. Move or delete large unnecessary files
4. If long-term, expand the partition or add storage

swappiness_ssd_wear.title: High swappiness on SSD — unnecessary write amplification
swappiness_ssd_wear.why: A high swappiness value causes the kernel to swap pages to disk aggressively even when RAM is available. On SSDs, each swap write counts against the drive's total write endurance (TBW). Sustained aggressive swapping shortens SSD lifespan, especially on entry-level drives.
swappiness_ssd_wear.how:
1. Check current value:
   cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness
2. Set a lower value immediately:
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10  # workstation
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=1   # server
3. Make permanent:
   echo 'vm.swappiness=1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: On a server with SSDs, high swappiness causes aggressive page swapping even when RAM is available, accelerating drive wear and increasing I/O latency. For database or I/O-intensive workloads, excessive swap activity can cause measurable performance degradation.

desktop.why: On a desktop with an SSD, high swappiness directly affects responsiveness and SSD longevity. The typical symptom is noticeable lag during memory-intensive tasks. Reducing swappiness to 10 is the standard recommendation for SSD desktops and has no downside.

container.why: Swappiness is a kernel-level setting controlled by the host. Container processes cannot modify vm.swappiness. This finding is not actionable inside a container — adjust vm.swappiness on the host system.
container.how:
Apply on the host system (not inside the container):
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10
   echo 'vm.swappiness=10' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

swappiness_unjustified.title: Swap in use despite abundant free RAM
swappiness_unjustified.why: The kernel is moving process memory to swap while RAM is largely available. This wastes swap write cycles (particularly damaging on SSDs), increases I/O latency for affected processes, and may indicate either a swappiness value that is too high for the workload or a memory leak in a running process.
swappiness_unjustified.how:
1. Identify processes with swapped-out memory:
   sudo smem -rs swap 2>/dev/null | head -15
2. Lower swappiness to reduce the tendency to swap:
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10
3. If a specific process is leaking memory, investigate:
   sudo top  # watch the RES/VIRT columns
4. Make swappiness permanent:
   echo 'vm.swappiness=10' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf

server.why: A server actively swapping while RAM is available indicates either a swappiness value too high for the workload or a memory-leaking process. Swap activity adds I/O latency and, on SSD-based servers, consumes write endurance. Investigate and tune.

desktop.why: On a desktop with sufficient RAM actively using swap, the first symptom is system sluggishness. Reducing swappiness from the default (60) to 10–20 improves responsiveness for typical desktop workloads without risking OOM events.

container.why: vm.swappiness cannot be tuned from within a container. If a container process is leaking memory, address the memory leak directly. For host-level swap tuning, apply the fix on the host.
container.how:
Investigate the memory-leaking process:
   docker stats <container>
For host-level swap tuning (apply on the host):
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10
   echo 'vm.swappiness=10' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

smb1_enabled.title: SMBv1 is enabled (EternalBlue / WannaCry vector)
smb1_enabled.why: SMBv1 is a 1990s protocol with multiple critical vulnerabilities. The NSA-developed EternalBlue exploit (leaked in 2017) targets SMBv1 and was used by WannaCry ransomware to infect over 200,000 systems in 150 countries in a single day. Microsoft deprecated SMBv1 in 2013. There is no legitimate reason to run SMBv1 today.
smb1_enabled.how:
1. Edit /etc/samba/smb.conf
2. In the [global] section add:
   min protocol = SMB2
3. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

null_passwords.title: Null passwords allowed (null passwords = yes)
null_passwords.why: Allows any account with no password set to authenticate to Samba with a blank password. An attacker only needs to know the username. Combined with guest or misconfigured accounts this grants immediate file system access with no credentials.
null_passwords.how:
1. Edit /etc/samba/smb.conf
2. In the [global] section set:
   null passwords = no
3. Ensure all accounts have passwords:
   sudo smbpasswd -a <user>
4. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

guest_writable.title: Guest-writable share (anonymous write access)
guest_writable.why: Any unauthenticated user on the network can upload, modify, or delete files in this share. This can be used to plant malware, exfiltrate data, or corrupt backups. Even on a trusted network, accidental or malicious modification without authentication creates serious integrity risks.
guest_writable.how:
1. Remove guest access entirely:
   [global] → map to guest = never
   [sharename] → remove 'guest ok = yes'
2. Or restrict to read-only:
   [sharename] → read only = yes
3. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

guest_readonly.title: Guest read-only share (anonymous read access)
guest_readonly.why: Any unauthenticated user on the network can read files from this share without providing credentials. While read-only access does not allow modification, it can be used for data exfiltration. Verify that all files in this share are intentionally public.
guest_readonly.how:
1. If anonymous access is not needed, remove guest access:
   [sharename] → remove 'guest ok = yes'
2. If read-only anonymous access is intentional, document it and ensure no sensitive data is in the share.
3. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

server_signing_disabled.title: Server signing disabled (NTLM relay attack vector)
server_signing_disabled.why: Without SMB signing, an attacker performing a man-in-the-middle attack can intercept and modify SMB traffic undetected, or relay NTLM authentication to other services. NTLM relay attacks are a standard technique in Active Directory penetration testing and real-world attacks (e.g. Responder, ntlmrelayx).
server_signing_disabled.how:
1. Edit /etc/samba/smb.conf
2. In the [global] section set:
   server signing = mandatory
3. Note: clients must also support signing (all modern clients do)
4. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

map_to_guest.title: map to guest = bad user (failed logins fall back to guest)
map_to_guest.why: When a user provides an invalid username, Samba silently logs them in as the guest account instead of returning an authentication error. This means an attacker who does not know a valid username still gets network access to all guest-accessible shares.
map_to_guest.how:
1. Edit /etc/samba/smb.conf
2. In the [global] section set:
   map to guest = never
3. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

db_very_outdated.title: Virus database critically outdated (> 30 days)
db_very_outdated.why: ClamAV's detection ability depends entirely on its signature database. An outdated database cannot detect malware discovered after the last update. Ransomware, trojans, and rootkits released in the past month would be completely invisible to the scanner.
db_very_outdated.how:
1. Update the database immediately:
   sudo freshclam
2. Enable automatic updates via the freshclam service:
   sudo systemctl enable --now clamav-freshclam
3. Verify cron or systemd timer is scheduling daily updates

server.why: An antivirus database older than 30 days on a server handling files (mail relay, upload service, shared storage) means recent malware strains are completely undetectable. Each day of delay adds hundreds of new undetectable signatures.

desktop.why: On a desktop, an outdated ClamAV database leaves you unprotected against recent malware. Since desktops handle user downloads, email attachments, and web content, keeping signatures current is essential for the tool to provide any meaningful protection.

container.why: ClamAV is rarely deployed in containers — scanning typically occurs at the host or gateway level, or via dedicated image scanners (Trivy, Snyk). If present, an outdated database in a container suggests the image rebuild cycle is not refreshing the database.

db_outdated.title: Virus database is outdated (> 7 days)
db_outdated.why: ClamAV releases new signature updates multiple times per day. After 7 days, hundreds of new malware signatures are missing from your database. This significantly reduces detection rates for recent threats.
db_outdated.how:
1. Update the database:
   sudo freshclam
2. Enable automatic daily updates:
   sudo systemctl enable --now clamav-freshclam
3. Check the freshclam timer:
   systemctl status clamav-freshclam

server.why: A ClamAV database 7–30 days old on a server is approaching the risk threshold. Automated freshclam updates should maintain the database without manual intervention — an outdated database suggests the automatic update process is failing.

desktop.why: On a desktop, a 7–30 day old database is a yellow flag. The freshclam daemon should handle updates automatically. If it is not running, re-enable it. Recent threats may be going undetected.

container.why: In a container, ClamAV database updates should be part of the image build pipeline. An outdated database in a running container indicates the image or update process needs review.

scan_very_old.title: Last scan is very old (> 90 days)
scan_very_old.why: Without regular scanning, infections can persist undetected for months. Linux systems are increasingly targeted by malware — web shells, crypto miners, backdoors, and rootkits do not announce themselves. Quarterly scans at minimum are needed to detect dormant infections.
scan_very_old.how:
1. Run an immediate scan of home directories:
   sudo clamscan -r /home --infected --log=/var/log/clamav/clamscan.log
2. Schedule weekly scans via cron:
   echo '0 2 * * 0 root clamscan -r /home --infected --log=/var/log/clamav/clamscan.log' | sudo tee /etc/cron.d/clamav-scan

server.why: If the last scan was over 90 days ago on a server handling files, malware may have been present for months. Web shells, crypto miners, and backdoors do not self-report. Run an immediate scan and establish regular weekly scans via cron.

desktop.why: A scan gap of 90+ days on a desktop means any malware received or downloaded during that period was not caught. Run an immediate scan and schedule weekly automated scans.

container.why: Periodic ClamAV scans inside containers are non-standard. Scanning typically occurs at the image build stage via tools like Trivy or Snyk. Manual ClamAV scans inside running containers are not a standard security practice in container pipelines.

scan_old.title: Last scan is over 30 days old
scan_old.why: Monthly scans leave a large window during which infections can establish persistence, exfiltrate data, or spread to other systems. On a server exposed to the internet, monthly scanning is insufficient.
scan_old.how:
1. Run a new scan:
   sudo clamscan -r /home --infected --log=/var/log/clamav/clamscan.log
2. Schedule weekly scans:
   echo '0 2 * * 0 root clamscan -r /home --infected --log=/var/log/clamav/clamscan.log' | sudo tee /etc/cron.d/clamav-scan

server.why: A 30–90 day scan gap on a server leaves a long window during which undetected malware could establish persistence. Increase scan frequency — weekly is the minimum recommended for production servers.

desktop.why: For a desktop, weekly scanning is a reasonable baseline. If it has been 30–90 days, re-enable the scheduled scan. Recent downloads or email attachments may have brought in undetected malware.

container.why: Same as scan_very_old — periodic ClamAV scans inside containers are non-standard. Focus on image security scanning (Trivy, Snyk) integrated into your CI/CD pipeline.

db_not_found.title: ClamAV is installed but its virus database is missing
db_not_found.why: ClamAV detects malware by matching files against a signature database (/var/lib/clamav/{main,daily,bytecode}.cvd). Without the database, the scanner cannot recognise anything — every scan returns clean. The most common cause is install + first-run failure: the freshclam service failed to download the initial signatures (rate-limited by the public mirrors, network blocked, /var/lib/clamav unwritable, or signature server outage at install time) and was never re-run.
db_not_found.how:
1. Run freshclam manually to download the database:
   sudo systemctl stop clamav-freshclam
   sudo freshclam --verbose
2. Restart the service:
   sudo systemctl start clamav-freshclam
3. Verify the database files exist:
   ls -lh /var/lib/clamav/
4. Trigger a scan to validate end-to-end:
   sudo clamscan --version
   sudo clamscan /tmp/

server.why: On a server, clamav with no database is misleading — the install looks complete but provides zero detection. Fix the freshclam download before treating clamav as a working defence.

desktop.why: On a desktop, the most likely cause is a captive Wi-Fi or rate-limited mirror at install time. Re-run freshclam once on a clean connection.

container.why: If ClamAV runs in a container, ensure the database volume is initialised. If it runs on the host, fix freshclam on the host.

freshclam_missing.title: ClamAV is installed but the freshclam updater service is not running
freshclam_missing.why: freshclam is the daemon (or cron job) that keeps the signature database current — without it, the database stagnates at whatever version was last fetched. ClamAV signatures are updated multiple times per day; a stalled freshclam means the scanner is blind to anything reported in the last hours or days. The most common cause is the service being masked or disabled by hand (often during a debug session) and forgotten.
freshclam_missing.how:
1. Verify the service exists and check its status:
   sudo systemctl status clamav-freshclam
2. Unmask if necessary:
   sudo systemctl unmask clamav-freshclam
3. Enable and start:
   sudo systemctl enable --now clamav-freshclam
4. Confirm freshclam is fetching updates:
   sudo journalctl -u clamav-freshclam -n 30

server.why: On a server, a stalled freshclam means production clamav misses every signature published since the last fetch. Enable the service; it has no significant resource cost.

desktop.why: On a desktop, the same applies — clamav is only as good as the latest signatures. Re-enable freshclam.

container.why: If ClamAV runs inside a container, freshclam should be in the container's process tree (or signatures shared from the host via volume). If on the host, re-enable there.

not_installed.title: Linux Audit Framework not installed
not_installed.why: auditd provides kernel-level logging of system calls, file access, authentication, and privileged commands. Without it, attackers can operate undetected — privilege escalations, unauthorized access, and sensitive file reads leave no forensic trace.
not_installed.how:
Install auditd and the dispatcher plugins:
  sudo apt install auditd audispd-plugins
  sudo systemctl enable --now auditd

Create a minimal rule set in /etc/audit/rules.d/99-local.rules:
  -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers

Load the rules:
  sudo augenrules --load

service_inactive.title: auditd installed but service not running
service_inactive.why: auditd is installed but stopped. Kernel events are not being logged in real time. Authentication events, sudo usage, and sensitive file access go unrecorded, eliminating forensic evidence if an incident occurs.
service_inactive.how:
Enable and start the service:
  sudo systemctl enable --now auditd

Verify it is running and rules are loaded:
  sudo systemctl status auditd
  sudo auditctl -l

no_rules.title: auditd running but no audit rules configured
no_rules.why: auditd is active but no rules are loaded. Only a minimal set of default events is captured. Critical events — access to /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, sudo invocations, privileged commands — go unlogged, making forensic analysis very difficult.
no_rules.how:
Create persistent rules in /etc/audit/rules.d/99-local.rules:
  -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers
  -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -k commands

Reload rules:
  sudo augenrules --load
  sudo systemctl restart auditd

Verify:
  sudo auditctl -l

missing_sensitive_rules.title: Sensitive files not covered by audit rules
missing_sensitive_rules.why: Critical files such as /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and /etc/sudoers are not monitored by auditd. Any unauthorized modification to these files could indicate privilege escalation or account takeover, and would leave no audit trail.
missing_sensitive_rules.how:
Add watch rules for the missing files in /etc/audit/rules.d/99-local.rules:
  -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers

Reload:
  sudo augenrules --load
  sudo systemctl restart auditd

server.why: On a server, unauthorized modifications to /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, or /etc/sudoers are high-severity indicators of privilege escalation or account takeover. Without watch rules for these files, such changes leave no audit trail — a critical gap for incident response and compliance.

desktop.why: Some sensitive files are not covered by auditd rules. On a desktop this is informational — these files are less frequently targeted — but adding watch rules provides an additional layer of forensic visibility.

setup_mode.title: Secure Boot is in Setup Mode (no Platform Key enrolled)
setup_mode.why: Secure Boot Setup Mode means no Platform Key is enrolled. Any bootloader, including a malicious one, can be loaded without verification. This effectively disables Secure Boot protections and allows persistent bootkits on systems with physical or early-boot access.
setup_mode.how:
Enroll your Platform Key via the UEFI firmware settings:
  1. Reboot and enter UEFI/BIOS (F2, F12, or Del).
  2. Navigate to Secure Boot → Key Management.
  3. Enroll a Platform Key (PK), Key Exchange Key (KEK), and database (db).

Alternatively, use mokutil to check state:
  mokutil --sb-state
  mokutil --enable-validation

disabled.title: Secure Boot is disabled
disabled.why: Secure Boot verifies that only trusted bootloaders and kernels load at startup. Without it, rootkits, bootkits, and malicious drivers can persist below the OS, bypassing all software-level defenses.
disabled.how:
Enable Secure Boot in your UEFI firmware settings:
  1. Reboot and enter UEFI/BIOS (F2, F12, or Del).
  2. Navigate to the Secure Boot settings.
  3. Set Secure Boot to Enabled.
  4. If you use custom kernels or third-party drivers, enroll a Machine Owner Key:
     sudo mokutil --import mok.der

server.why: Secure Boot is disabled. On servers this is common — cloud images, out-of-tree drivers (NVIDIA, ZFS), and custom kernels often require it to be disabled. This is noted for completeness; no score deduction is applied for server profiles.
server.how:
No action is required on server profiles. If you want to enable Secure Boot, ensure all loaded kernels and modules are signed, then enable it in UEFI settings. Use mokutil to enroll custom signing keys if needed:
  mokutil --sb-state
  mokutil --import mok.der

desktop.why: On a desktop, disabling Secure Boot allows rootkits, bootkits, and malicious drivers to load before the OS, bypassing all software-level defenses. This is a real threat vector for persistent, kernel-level attacks, especially on laptops or shared workstations.

not_installed.title: No file integrity monitoring tool installed
not_installed.why: Without a file integrity monitor (AIDE or Tripwire), there is no way to detect unauthorized modifications to system files, configuration files, or binaries. An attacker who gains access can replace binaries, add backdoors, or alter configuration without detection.
not_installed.how:
Install and initialize AIDE:
  sudo apt install aide
  sudo aideinit                    # creates the initial baseline database
  sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db

Schedule regular checks in cron:
  echo '0 3 * * * root /usr/bin/aide --check 2>&1 | mail -s "AIDE check" root' | sudo tee /etc/cron.d/aide-check

no_db.title: File integrity tool installed but no baseline database
no_db.why: The integrity monitoring tool is installed but no baseline database has been created. Without a baseline, the tool cannot detect changes to system files. Any modifications made before database initialization will never be flagged.
no_db.how:
Initialize the baseline database:
  For AIDE:     sudo aideinit && sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db
  For Tripwire: sudo tripwire --init

Then schedule regular checks:
  sudo crontab -e
  0 3 * * * /usr/bin/aide --check 2>&1 | mail -s 'AIDE report' root

no_check.title: Integrity baseline exists but no check has ever been run
no_check.why: A baseline database exists but no integrity check has been performed since initialization. Without regular checks, any file modification since baseline creation — including malicious ones — goes undetected.
no_check.how:
Run an integrity check immediately:
  For AIDE:     sudo aide --check
  For Tripwire: sudo tripwire --check

If the output shows unexpected changes, investigate each one. Schedule regular checks:
  sudo crontab -e
  0 3 * * * /usr/bin/aide --check 2>&1 | mail -s 'AIDE report' root

check_old.title: File integrity check has not been run recently
check_old.why: The last file integrity check is outdated. Recent changes to system files — legitimate or malicious — have not been verified against the baseline. Integrity monitoring loses its value if checks are not performed regularly.
check_old.how:
Run a new integrity check:
  For AIDE:     sudo aide --check
  For Tripwire: sudo tripwire --check

Automate regular checks:
  sudo crontab -e
  0 3 * * * /usr/bin/aide --check 2>&1 | mail -s 'AIDE report' root

After verifying all known-good changes, update the baseline:
  sudo aide --update && sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db

bypass_risk.title: Virtualisation bridge may bypass UFW FORWARD policy
bypass_risk.why: Hypervisors such as libvirt/KVM, VirtualBox, and VMware create Linux bridge interfaces (virbr0, vboxnet*, etc.) and inject their own iptables rules directly into the FORWARD chain. These rules can allow traffic between VMs and the host — or between VMs and the internet — independently of UFW's FORWARD policy. UFW manages only its own ruleset and cannot prevent bridge-injected rules from permitting forwarded traffic.
bypass_risk.how:
Audit the FORWARD rules inserted by the bridge:
  sudo iptables -L FORWARD -v --line-numbers | grep virbr0

This is expected behaviour for a VM host — review the output to confirm only legitimate VM traffic is forwarded.

To isolate VMs from the internet while keeping local host access, configure libvirt's network in isolated mode:
  virsh net-edit default  # set <forward mode='none'/> for isolated networks

If you no longer use virtual machines:
  sudo systemctl disable --now libvirtd

snap_network.title: Snap-based virtualisation tool detected (multipass, lxd-snap) — network surface review needed
snap_network.why: Snap-packaged virtualisation tools (multipass, lxd) install their own bridge interfaces and inject FORWARD-chain rules similar to libvirt/KVM, but via the snap confinement model rather than the system package manager. They are easy to install and easy to forget — the bridge persists across snap upgrades, and the host's UFW FORWARD policy does not control inter-VM or VM-to-internet traffic on these bridges. The 'snap version' is also harder to discover with standard package audits (dpkg -l misses them).
snap_network.how:
1. Inventory snap-installed virt tools:
   snap list | grep -Ei 'multipass|lxd'
2. Inspect the bridge interfaces and their iptables rules:
   ip link show | grep -Ei 'lxd|mpqemubr'
   sudo iptables -L FORWARD -v | grep -Ei 'lxd|mpqemubr'
3. If you no longer use the tool, remove it (and the bridge cleans up):
   sudo snap remove --purge multipass
   sudo snap remove --purge lxd
4. If you keep it, document the bridge in your firewall posture and accept that UFW does not gate its FORWARD chain.

server.why: On a server, an unused snap-installed virt tool is dormant attack surface and a forgotten bridge. Audit and remove if unused.

desktop.why: On a desktop, multipass / lxd via snap is common for dev workflows. Just be aware the bridge sits outside UFW's view; treat the VMs themselves as trusted endpoints.

container.why: Snap is rarely available inside containers; this finding is a host concern.

brute_force.title: Brute-force attacks detected in authentication logs
brute_force.why: Repeated failed login attempts indicate active automated attacks against this machine. If password authentication or weak credentials are in use, persistent brute-force campaigns will eventually succeed. Even with strong passwords, flood attacks consume CPU and lock out legitimate users.
brute_force.how:
1. Install and configure fail2ban:
   sudo apt install fail2ban
   sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
2. Verify the SSH jail is active:
   sudo fail2ban-client status sshd
3. Disable password authentication (use keys only):
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PasswordAuthentication no
4. Reduce MaxAuthTries:
   MaxAuthTries 3
5. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

public_login.title: Successful logins from public IP addresses detected
public_login.why: Remote logins from public IPs visible in auth logs confirm the machine is internet-reachable and actively accessed. Any credential compromise — brute force, stolen key, leaked password — would give an attacker an immediate shell on a live system.
public_login.how:
1. Restrict SSH access to known IPs via UFW:
   sudo ufw allow from <your-ip> to any port 22
   sudo ufw delete allow 22
2. Use key-only authentication:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PasswordAuthentication no
3. Review who is logging in:
   sudo last | head -20
4. Consider a VPN or port-knocking if remote access must be maintained

world_writable.title: Default umask allows world-writable file creation (umask 0000 or 0002)
world_writable.why: A world-writable umask means every new file created by any user is writable by all users on the system. Attackers with any local account can modify scripts, configs, and data files created by privileged processes — enabling privilege escalation and persistent backdoors.
world_writable.how:
1. Set a secure default umask in /etc/profile and /etc/bash.bashrc:
   umask 0022
2. For stricter environments:
   umask 0027
3. Verify the change takes effect:
   umask  # should return 0022 or stricter
4. Check /etc/login.defs:
   UMASK 022

group_writable.title: Default umask allows group-writable file creation (umask 002)
group_writable.why: A group-writable umask means every new file is writable by any member of the creating user's group. On multi-user systems or systems with shared service accounts, this can allow horizontal privilege escalation between users sharing a group.
group_writable.how:
1. Set umask to 0022 in /etc/profile:
   umask 0022
2. Verify:
   umask  # should return 0022

ufw_missing.title: UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is not installed
ufw_missing.why: Without a host firewall, every listening service on the machine is exposed to whatever network it is connected to. There is no per-service allow/deny policy, no inbound default-deny, and no rule audit trail. On an internet-exposed host this is a critical gap; on a LAN-only host it still leaves the system trivially reachable by any compromised peer.
ufw_missing.how:
1. Install UFW:
   sudo apt install ufw
2. Set the safe default policy:
   sudo ufw default deny incoming
   sudo ufw default allow outgoing
3. (If you use SSH) allow it before enabling:
   sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
4. Enable the firewall:
   sudo ufw enable
5. Verify:
   sudo ufw status verbose

inactive.title: UFW firewall is installed but inactive
inactive.why: UFW is present on the system but disabled. The configured rules (if any) are not enforced — incoming connections are filtered only by whatever underlying iptables/nftables state happens to be active. This usually means no host-level filtering at all: a reboot, network change, or misconfigured iptables rule will leave the system fully exposed. The status is also misleading: 'ufw installed' suggests protection that does not exist.
inactive.how:
1. Verify the inactive state:
   sudo ufw status
2. Make sure SSH (or whatever you need to keep reachable) is allowed before enabling:
   sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
3. Enable the firewall:
   sudo ufw enable
4. Verify it is now active:
   sudo ufw status verbose
5. Confirm it starts on boot:
   sudo systemctl is-enabled ufw

policy_open.title: UFW default incoming policy is ALLOW (all ports open by default)
policy_open.why: When the default policy is set to ALLOW, every port is reachable unless an explicit deny rule blocks it. This inverts the standard security model: instead of opening the few services you need, you must enumerate and close every service you don't. New services (a freshly installed daemon, a new container) become reachable immediately with no allowlist gate. A single forgotten port is enough for a compromise.
policy_open.how:
1. Switch to deny-by-default for incoming traffic:
   sudo ufw default deny incoming
2. Keep outgoing allowed (or restrict if your policy requires it):
   sudo ufw default allow outgoing
3. Re-allow the specific services you genuinely need:
   sudo ufw allow 22/tcp           # SSH
   sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 445  # Samba on LAN only
4. Verify:
   sudo ufw status verbose

policy_unknown.title: UFW default incoming policy could not be determined
policy_unknown.why: BOB queried ufw status verbose but could not parse the default policy line. This usually means UFW is in an unexpected state (output format differs, version too old, or the service is partly broken). A firewall with an undetermined policy cannot be trusted: you do not know whether the default is deny or allow, so you do not know which ports are currently reachable.
policy_unknown.how:
1. Inspect the raw status output manually:
   sudo ufw status verbose
2. Look for the line: 'Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), deny (routed)'
3. If the Default line is missing or malformed, reset to a known state:
   sudo ufw disable
   sudo ufw reset    # clears all rules — re-add them afterwards
   sudo ufw default deny incoming
   sudo ufw default allow outgoing
   sudo ufw enable
4. Verify UFW version (older versions output differently):
   ufw --version

logging_off.title: UFW firewall logging is disabled
logging_off.why: Without firewall logs, blocked connection attempts, port scans, and intrusion attempts leave no trace. Forensic investigation after an incident becomes impossible — you cannot determine when an attack started, which ports were probed, or where traffic came from.
logging_off.how:
1. Enable UFW logging:
   sudo ufw logging on
2. For more detail:
   sudo ufw logging medium
   # or: sudo ufw logging high
3. Verify:
   sudo ufw status verbose | grep Logging
4. Logs appear in:
   /var/log/ufw.log  (or journald)

expired.title: TLS/SSL certificate has expired
expired.why: An expired certificate causes browsers and clients to display hard trust errors and refuse connections. Services may become completely inaccessible. Expired certificates are also a signal of poor certificate lifecycle management — attackers specifically look for expired certificates to exploit.
expired.how:
1. Identify which certificate is expired:
   sudo bob --check ssl_certs --verbose
2. For Let's Encrypt:
   sudo certbot renew --force-renewal
3. For manually managed certificates:
   openssl x509 -in /path/to/cert.pem -noout -dates
   Replace with a new certificate from your CA
4. Verify:
   openssl x509 -in /path/to/cert.pem -noout -enddate

expiring_critical.title: TLS/SSL certificate expires within 7 days
expiring_critical.why: A certificate expiring in under a week requires immediate action. Once expired, services stop working for all clients. Automated renewal may have failed silently — manual intervention is needed now to avoid an outage.
expiring_critical.how:
1. For Let's Encrypt:
   sudo certbot renew --force-renewal
   sudo systemctl reload nginx  # or apache2
2. Check renewal timer:
   sudo systemctl status certbot.timer
3. For manual certs, contact your CA immediately for a replacement
4. Verify the new expiry:
   openssl x509 -in /path/to/cert.pem -noout -enddate

expiring_soon.title: TLS/SSL certificate expires within 30 days
expiring_soon.why: Certificates expiring in under a month need attention before they expire. Automated renewal tools (certbot, acme.sh) should have already renewed them. A failure to renew automatically often indicates a misconfigured renewal job or DNS/port issue.
expiring_soon.how:
1. Force-renew Let's Encrypt certificates:
   sudo certbot renew
2. Check renewal logs:
   sudo journalctl -u certbot
3. Verify timer is active:
   sudo systemctl status certbot.timer
4. For manual certificates, request a renewal from your CA

pipe_to_shell.title: Systemd timer unit pipes downloaded content to a shell
pipe_to_shell.why: Piping curl or wget output directly to bash/sh executes arbitrary code from a remote server without any integrity verification. If the remote server is compromised, misconfigured, or the connection is intercepted, an attacker can execute any command as the user running the timer.
pipe_to_shell.how:
1. Identify the timer unit:
   sudo bob --check systemd_timers --verbose
2. Edit the unit to download first, verify, then execute:
   systemctl edit <unit>.service
3. Use checksums or package managers instead of curl-to-shell patterns
4. Consider using signed packages or configuration management tools

world_writable.title: Systemd timer ExecStart script is world-writable
world_writable.why: Any local user can modify a world-writable script that is executed by a privileged systemd timer. This is a direct privilege escalation path — write your code into the script and wait for the timer to fire as root.
world_writable.how:
1. Fix permissions on the script:
   sudo chmod 755 /path/to/script.sh
   sudo chown root:root /path/to/script.sh
2. Verify:
   ls -la /path/to/script.sh  # should show -rwxr-xr-x root root
3. Audit all timer scripts regularly:
   find /etc/systemd/system -name '*.service' | xargs grep -l ExecStart

user_created_root.title: User-created systemd timer runs as root
user_created_root.why: A non-package timer running as root that was created by a regular user is a strong indicator of a persistence mechanism or privilege escalation backdoor. Legitimate system services are installed by packages; user-created root timers are unusual and warrant immediate investigation.
user_created_root.how:
1. Identify and inspect the timer:
   systemctl list-timers --all
   systemctl cat <suspicious-timer>.service
2. Check who created the file:
   ls -la /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.service
3. If not a known legitimate service, disable and remove:
   sudo systemctl disable --now <unit>.timer
   sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.*

fwupd_updates.title: Firmware updates available via fwupd
fwupd_updates.why: Firmware vulnerabilities (UEFI, NVMe, Thunderbolt, etc.) run below the operating system and cannot be patched by the OS. Unpatched firmware enables persistent rootkits that survive OS reinstallation, and can bypass Secure Boot, TPM attestation, and kernel mitigations.
fwupd_updates.how:
1. List available firmware updates:
   fwupdmgr get-updates
2. Apply updates:
   sudo fwupdmgr update
3. Reboot if required:
   sudo reboot
4. Automate future checks:
   sudo systemctl enable --now fwupd-refresh.timer

microcode_missing.title: CPU microcode update package not installed
microcode_missing.why: CPU microcode patches critical hardware vulnerabilities including Spectre, Meltdown, MDS, TAA, and many others. Without microcode updates, these side-channel attacks can allow unprivileged processes to read kernel memory, cross VM boundaries, and extract cryptographic keys.
microcode_missing.how:
1. Install the appropriate microcode package:
   # Intel CPU:
   sudo apt install intel-microcode
   # AMD CPU:
   sudo apt install amd64-microcode
2. Reboot to apply:
   sudo reboot
3. Verify microcode is loaded:
   grep microcode /proc/cpuinfo | head -1

aslr_disabled.title: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomisation) is disabled
aslr_disabled.why: ASLR randomises the memory address layout of processes, making it significantly harder to exploit memory corruption vulnerabilities (buffer overflows, use-after-free). Without ASLR, an attacker can predict the exact address of shellcode, ROP gadgets, and heap allocations, making exploits far more reliable.
aslr_disabled.how:
1. Enable ASLR permanently:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=2
   echo 'kernel.randomize_va_space = 2' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-aslr.conf
2. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space  # should return 2

aslr_conservative.title: ASLR set to conservative mode (randomize_va_space=1)
aslr_conservative.why: Conservative ASLR (value 1) randomises stack and mmap() allocations but not the heap. Heap spray and heap-based exploitation techniques remain more reliable against a target with conservative ASLR than with full ASLR (value 2).
aslr_conservative.how:
1. Enable full ASLR:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=2
   echo 'kernel.randomize_va_space = 2' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-aslr.conf
2. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space  # should return 2

ptrace_unrestricted.title: ptrace is unrestricted (kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0)
ptrace_unrestricted.why: With unrestricted ptrace, any process can attach to and read/write the memory of any other process owned by the same user. An attacker with a low-privilege shell can extract credentials from browser sessions, SSH agents, gpg-agent, and sudo credential caches running in the same user session.
ptrace_unrestricted.how:
1. Restrict ptrace to parent processes only:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1
   echo 'kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-ptrace.conf
2. For stricter environments (admins only):
   kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 2
3. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope

dmesg_exposed.title: Kernel log (dmesg) accessible by unprivileged users
dmesg_exposed.why: The kernel ring buffer contains memory addresses, driver information, device names, and sometimes credentials passed as kernel parameters. Unprivileged access to dmesg significantly helps attackers defeat ASLR, identify kernel version and modules, and find attack surface.
dmesg_exposed.how:
1. Restrict dmesg to root:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.dmesg_restrict=1
   echo 'kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-dmesg.conf
2. Verify:
