   cat /proc/sys/kernel/dmesg_restrict  # should return 1

kptr_exposed.title: Kernel pointer addresses exposed to unprivileged users (kptr_restrict=0)
kptr_exposed.why: Kernel pointer addresses in /proc/kallsyms, /proc/modules, and similar interfaces help attackers locate kernel code and data structures when attempting kernel exploitation. Exposing them makes bypassing kernel ASLR much easier.
kptr_exposed.how:
1. Restrict kernel pointer exposure:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.kptr_restrict=2
   echo 'kernel.kptr_restrict = 2' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-kptr.conf
2. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/kernel/kptr_restrict  # should return 1 or 2

suid_dump_all.title: Core dumps enabled for SUID processes (fs.suid_dumpable=2)
suid_dump_all.why: When suid_dumpable is set to 2, SUID processes can produce core dumps readable by all users. Core dumps of SUID programs contain the full process memory — including any secrets, keys, or elevated-privilege data held in memory at crash time.
suid_dump_all.how:
1. Disable SUID core dumps:
   sudo sysctl -w fs.suid_dumpable=0
   echo 'fs.suid_dumpable = 0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-suid-dump.conf
2. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/fs/suid_dumpable  # should return 0

unexpected_suid.title: Unexpected SUID binary detected
unexpected_suid.why: SUID (Set User ID) binaries execute with the file owner's privileges (typically root) regardless of who runs them. An unexpected SUID binary is either a privilege escalation backdoor planted by an attacker, or a legitimate tool left SUID unnecessarily. Either way, it represents an uncontrolled root execution path.
unexpected_suid.how:
1. Identify all SUID binaries:
   find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
2. For each unexpected binary, investigate its origin:
   dpkg -S /path/to/binary
3. Remove the SUID bit if not required:
   sudo chmod u-s /path/to/binary
4. If the binary is unknown or suspicious:
   sha256sum /path/to/binary
   # Compare with known-good hash from the vendor

unexpected_sgid.title: Unexpected SGID binary detected
unexpected_sgid.why: SGID (Set Group ID) binaries execute with the file's group privileges. An unexpected SGID binary can provide access to privileged group resources (shadow, disk, docker, sudo) for any user who runs it — enabling group-level privilege escalation.
unexpected_sgid.how:
1. Identify all SGID binaries:
   find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null
2. Investigate each unexpected binary:
   dpkg -S /path/to/binary
3. Remove the SGID bit if not required:
   sudo chmod g-s /path/to/binary

escalated_posture.title: Risk level raised by posture (firewall structural gap)
escalated_posture.why: BOB derives the displayed risk level from the global score combined with the posture state. Pre-v0.7.0 the level was score-only — a host with UFW inactive but otherwise clean (score 8/10) displayed 'LOW risk', misleading operators about the actual exposure. v0.7.0 introduces a posture floor: when the firewall is structurally broken (inactive, INPUT ACCEPT, or firewall domain ≤ 3/10), the level is lifted out of LOW to reflect that the host is reachable on any port regardless of the cleanliness of the rest. The base score still drives the value; posture only raises the floor.
escalated_posture.how:
1. Identify which posture trigger fired (look at the parenthetical annotation next to the risk level):
   - 'firewall inactive' → enable UFW: sudo ufw enable
   - 'iptables INPUT ACCEPT' → set deny default: sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP (or migrate to UFW)
   - 'firewall domain low' → review the firewall section findings (rules, logging, default policy)
2. Re-run the audit:
   sudo bob
3. The risk level returns to its score-derived value once the posture trigger no longer fires.

pipe_to_shell.title: Pipe-to-shell pattern in system cron (curl/wget | sh)
pipe_to_shell.why: Fetching a script and piping it directly to a shell bypasses all integrity checks. If the remote server is compromised, the DNS is hijacked, or the connection is intercepted (plain HTTP), arbitrary code runs with the cron job's privileges — often root. There is no way to audit or version-control what will be executed at runtime.
pipe_to_shell.how:
1. Identify the cron entry in /etc/cron.* or /etc/crontab
2. Replace with a two-step approach:
   a. Download to a file: curl -fsSL -o /tmp/script.sh https://...
   b. Verify checksum: sha256sum -c /tmp/script.sha256
   c. Execute: bash /tmp/script.sh
3. Better: host the script locally, pin it in version control,
   and reference the local copy from cron

world_writable.title: World-writable script referenced in system cron
world_writable.why: Any local user can modify a world-writable script. Because cron runs it on a schedule — often as root — overwriting the script is a trivial local privilege escalation: no exploit needed, just write access to the file. This is a classic persistence and escalation technique.
world_writable.how:
1. Remove world-write permission:
   sudo chmod o-w <path>
2. Verify ownership is correct (should be root):
   ls -la <path>
3. Review the script content for unexpected modifications:
   sudo cat <path>

privileged.title: Docker container running in privileged mode
privileged.why: A privileged container has full access to the host's devices and capabilities — it is effectively running as root on the host with all restrictions removed. Any process inside a privileged container can escape to the host, modify kernel parameters, mount host filesystems, and compromise the entire system.
privileged.how:
1. Identify the privileged container:
   docker ps --quiet | xargs docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} privileged={{.HostConfig.Privileged}}'
2. Remove the --privileged flag and grant only the specific capabilities needed:
   docker run --cap-add NET_ADMIN (instead of --privileged)
3. If the container genuinely needs privileged access, isolate it on a dedicated host
4. Use seccomp profiles and AppArmor policies

root_containers.title: Docker containers running as root (no user namespace remapping)
root_containers.why: Containers running as UID 0 inside the container map directly to root on the host when user namespace remapping is not configured. A container escape vulnerability — of which Docker has had several — gives an attacker immediate root on the host.
root_containers.how:
1. Add a non-root USER in your Dockerfile:
   USER 1000:1000
2. Or enable user namespace remapping globally:
   sudo nano /etc/docker/daemon.json
   { "userns-remap": "default" }
   sudo systemctl restart docker
3. Verify:
   docker run alpine id  # should not return uid=0

socket_mounted.title: Docker socket mounted inside a container
socket_mounted.why: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container gives it full control of the Docker daemon — and therefore the host. From inside the container, an attacker can start a new privileged container, mount the host filesystem, and escape with a single docker command. This is a complete container isolation bypass.
socket_mounted.how:
1. Remove the socket mount from the container:
   Remove -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock from docker run
2. If the container needs to manage Docker (CI agents, Portainer), use:
   - Docker-in-Docker (dind) with explicit isolation
   - A Docker TCP socket with TLS authentication instead of the Unix socket
3. Audit running containers:
   docker ps -q | xargs docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}: {{.Mounts}}' | grep docker.sock

host_network.title: Docker container using host network mode
host_network.why: A container with --network=host shares the host's network namespace entirely. It can bind to any port on the host, listen on all interfaces, and access any network service running on localhost. Network-based container isolation does not exist for such containers.
host_network.how:
1. Remove --network=host and use explicit port publishing:
   docker run -p 8080:80 myimage  (instead of --network=host)
2. If host networking is required for performance (e.g. latency-sensitive apps), restrict capabilities and use AppArmor/seccomp profiles
3. Audit host-networked containers:
   docker ps -q | xargs docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}: {{.HostConfig.NetworkMode}}' | grep host

service_inactive.title: Security service enabled at boot but currently inactive
service_inactive.why: A service configured to start at boot but currently stopped may have crashed, been misconfigured, or been deliberately disabled. If the service is a security control (firewall, intrusion detection, log daemon), its absence creates a window during which threats go undetected or unblocked. The system appears protected at startup but is not at runtime.
service_inactive.how:
1. Check why the service stopped:
   sudo journalctl -u <service> -n 50
2. Restart and verify:
   sudo systemctl start <service>
   sudo systemctl status <service>
3. If the service crashes on start, investigate the config:
   sudo systemctl status <service> --no-pager -l
4. Ensure it remains enabled:
   sudo systemctl enable <service>

server.why: A service enabled at boot but currently inactive on a server may indicate a crashed or misconfigured security control. It will restart at next boot, potentially exposing a port that appears closed right now. On a server, investigate and resolve immediately.

desktop.why: On a desktop, an enabled-but-inactive service is typically a leftover from an old installation. While the risk is lower (no inbound exposure expected), it wastes startup time and may cause subtle issues. Disable unused services as a hygiene measure.

container.why: In a container, systemd is often not the init system. If your container uses a lightweight init (s6, runit, supervisord), this finding may not apply. If systemd is present in the container, follow the server guidance.

no_backend.title: No firewall backend present (no iptables, no nftables)
no_backend.why: Without iptables or nftables installed and active, the kernel has no firewall rules at all — every port reachable from the network is fully exposed. UFW (or any other userspace firewall) ultimately relies on one of these backends to write rules into the kernel. Missing both means the system is operating without any packet filter whatsoever.
no_backend.how:
1. Install iptables (or nftables) on the system:
   sudo apt install iptables
2. After install, configure UFW or another front-end and enable it:
   sudo apt install ufw && sudo ufw enable
3. Verify rules are loaded:
   sudo iptables -L -n  # or: sudo nft list ruleset

server.why: A server with no firewall backend is fully exposed to the network — there is no kernel-level filtering, no default deny, no ability to restrict any service. This is one of the worst possible postures for any networked machine.

desktop.why: Even behind NAT, a desktop without iptables/nftables has no defence against local-network attacks (peer devices, malicious neighbours on shared Wi-Fi). Installing a backend + UFW is universally recommended.

container.why: Containers usually inherit packet filtering from the host. This finding suggests the host has no firewall — fix on the host system.
container.how:
Install on the host system:
   sudo apt install iptables ufw
   sudo ufw enable

input_accept.title: Default INPUT policy is ACCEPT (every unfiltered packet is allowed in)
input_accept.why: The INPUT chain policy is the firewall's final fallback when no explicit rule matches an incoming packet. When set to ACCEPT, every port that has no specific DROP/REJECT rule is open to the network — the default is permissive. The secure pattern is policy=DROP combined with explicit ACCEPT rules for permitted services, so anything not whitelisted is automatically blocked.
input_accept.how:
1. Apply default-deny immediately. Before flipping the policy, make sure you have explicit ACCEPT rules for loopback and for any service you depend on (notably SSH) — otherwise you will lock yourself out:
   sudo iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT
   sudo iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
   sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT   # keep SSH reachable
   sudo iptables -P INPUT DROP
2. Save the rules so they persist after reboot (iptables-persistent on Debian/Ubuntu):
   sudo apt install iptables-persistent
   sudo netfilter-persistent save
3. For nftables-based systems, use:
   sudo nft chain inet filter input '{ policy drop; }'

server.why: On a server, INPUT=ACCEPT means every newly opened socket is reachable from any source until you manually add a DROP rule for it. A default-deny policy is mandatory for any production server. Forgetting one explicit DROP today is forgetting one open port tomorrow.

desktop.why: On a desktop behind NAT, external exposure is mitigated by the router, but local-segment attacks (other devices on the same Wi-Fi) still reach the machine. Default-deny is the standard hardening pattern even for clients.

container.why: iptables policy is set by the host or by the container runtime; inside a default container you cannot change it. Adjust the container's network policy at the runtime level, or set the host policy.

forward_accept.title: Default FORWARD policy is ACCEPT (router-like behaviour by default)
forward_accept.why: The FORWARD chain handles packets routed THROUGH the host (not destined to local processes). FORWARD=ACCEPT means the kernel will forward any packet by default if IP forwarding is also enabled — turning the machine into a routing hop for anything that asks. Combined with a misconfigured network, this can be used to bridge segments or exfiltrate traffic via the host. The safe default for a non-router is policy=DROP.
forward_accept.how:
1. Set FORWARD policy to DROP:
   sudo iptables -P FORWARD DROP
   # or with nftables:
   sudo nft chain inet filter forward '{ policy drop; }'
2. Make it persistent (iptables-persistent on Debian/Ubuntu):
   sudo netfilter-persistent save
3. If this machine actually performs routing (libvirt host with virbr0, Docker host, KVM gateway, …), keep FORWARD=ACCEPT but ensure the application-layer firewall (UFW, libvirt rules) provides the filtering — and revisit the routing chains explicitly with 'sudo iptables -L FORWARD -n'.

server.why: A standard application server should not forward traffic — FORWARD=DROP is the safe default. The exception is virtualisation or container hosts (libvirt, Docker, KVM, LXC) which legitimately route guest traffic — in that case the policy is intentionally permissive but the rule chains must compensate.

desktop.why: A desktop is virtually never a router. Letting FORWARD=ACCEPT is unnecessary attack surface and can be abused if the desktop is bridged or shares its network connection. DROP is safe.

container.why: Containers should not be forwarding hosts. FORWARD policy is configured at the host level; address it there.
container.how:
Apply on the container host:
   sudo iptables -P FORWARD DROP
   sudo netfilter-persistent save

no_loopback.title: INPUT default-deny without a loopback ACCEPT rule
no_loopback.why: When INPUT policy is DROP, the loopback interface (127.0.0.1 / lo) is also dropped unless an explicit ACCEPT rule exists. Many local services rely on loopback: postgres listening on localhost, web apps talking to a local backend, system daemons communicating over 127.0.0.1. Without the loopback exception, these break silently — and you may not notice until a specific local process fails.
no_loopback.how:
1. Insert a loopback ACCEPT rule at the top of INPUT:
   sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -i lo -j ACCEPT
   # or with nftables:
   sudo nft insert rule inet filter input iif "lo" accept
2. Make persistent:
   sudo netfilter-persistent save
3. Verify loopback works (curl a local service that listens on 127.0.0.1).

server.why: Almost every server runs at least one service that binds to 127.0.0.1 (PostgreSQL, Redis, fcgi sockets, supervisord interfaces). Missing the loopback rule breaks them silently and causes long debugging sessions. It is the single most common omission when a fresh default-deny policy is applied.

desktop.why: Many desktop applications (browsers, IDEs, dev tools, system trays) talk to local services over loopback. Without the explicit ACCEPT rule, these silently fail. Add the loopback rule before tightening INPUT.

container.why: Loopback INSIDE a container is handled by the container's own network namespace and is unaffected by host iptables rules. This finding applies to the host's INPUT chain — fix on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo iptables -I INPUT 1 -i lo -j ACCEPT
   sudo netfilter-persistent save

no_conntrack.title: INPUT default-deny without an ESTABLISHED,RELATED ACCEPT rule
no_conntrack.why: With INPUT policy=DROP, return packets from outbound connections (web browser fetching a page, apt downloading updates, ssh client receiving server response) are dropped along with everything else unless an explicit rule accepts conntrack-tracked ESTABLISHED and RELATED states. The result is that the machine can open outbound connections but never receive any reply — effectively cutting off all client-side network usage.
no_conntrack.how:
1. Insert the conntrack rule near the top of INPUT (right after loopback):
   sudo iptables -I INPUT 2 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
   # or with nftables:
   sudo nft insert rule inet filter input ct state established,related accept
2. Make persistent:
   sudo netfilter-persistent save
3. Verify outbound usage works (curl https://example.com).

server.why: A server with INPUT=DROP but no conntrack ACCEPT cannot complete its own outbound HTTP requests, package updates, or DNS lookups. The fix is mandatory for any default-deny INPUT configuration.

desktop.why: Without the conntrack rule, every outbound request (web browsing, downloads, package management) appears to hang and time out because the responses are silently dropped. It is the most common cause of "after enabling firewall, internet broke".

container.why: Container network namespaces have their own conntrack handling. This finding refers to the host INPUT chain — fix on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo iptables -I INPUT 2 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
   sudo netfilter-persistent save

iptables_bypass.title: Raw iptables ACCEPT rule in INPUT bypasses UFW filtering
iptables_bypass.why: UFW writes its rules into dedicated chains (ufw-before-input, ufw-input, ufw-after-input). A raw ACCEPT rule sitting directly in the INPUT chain takes effect BEFORE the ufw-* chains are reached, so packets matching it are allowed in regardless of any UFW deny rule that would otherwise reject them. The result is a silent UFW bypass — `ufw status` shows the firewall as active and configured, while traffic for the bypassed port flows freely. These rules are typically left over from manual iptables tweaks or from a previously-installed package.
iptables_bypass.how:
1. List the offending rules:
   sudo iptables -L INPUT -n --line-numbers
2. Delete each raw ACCEPT rule (replace N with the line number):
   sudo iptables -D INPUT N
3. If the rule was added by a package or a startup script, find and disable the source — otherwise it will reappear after reboot:
   sudo grep -r 'iptables -A INPUT' /etc/
4. Save the cleaned ruleset:
   sudo netfilter-persistent save

server.why: On a server, a raw INPUT ACCEPT rule means part of your firewall posture is invisible to UFW management — `ufw allow` and `ufw deny` cannot affect it. The exposed port stays open whatever the documented UFW config says.

desktop.why: On a desktop, the same problem applies: UFW reports the system as protected while the bypass rule keeps a port reachable. Audit and remove any raw rule you did not add intentionally.

container.why: INPUT chain rules live on the host. Inspect the host's iptables and reconcile with UFW there.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo iptables -L INPUT -n --line-numbers
   sudo iptables -D INPUT N   # for each offending rule

iptables_forward_bypass.title: Raw iptables ACCEPT rule in FORWARD bypasses UFW filtering (no routing daemon detected)
iptables_forward_bypass.why: Same pattern as iptables_bypass but on the FORWARD chain. ACCEPT rules in FORWARD allow routed traffic (packets transiting through the host) to pass without being filtered by UFW's ufw-forward chain. Docker, libvirt and WireGuard legitimately add such rules — but those daemons are NOT detected on this system, so the rule is unexpected. It typically means a removed package left orphan rules behind, or a manual debugging session was forgotten.
iptables_forward_bypass.how:
1. List the FORWARD rules:
   sudo iptables -L FORWARD -n --line-numbers
2. Delete each unexpected ACCEPT rule:
   sudo iptables -D FORWARD N
3. Find the source and disable it (similar to iptables_bypass):
   sudo grep -r 'iptables -A FORWARD' /etc/
4. Save the cleaned ruleset:
   sudo netfilter-persistent save

server.why: On a non-routing server, FORWARD ACCEPT rules should not exist. If they do, they expose any neighbour-network traffic to free transit through the host — a routing vector that can be abused for traffic relay or NAT puncturing.

desktop.why: A desktop should never forward traffic. Orphan FORWARD ACCEPT rules typically come from a removed VPN client or container runtime. Remove them once you have confirmed nothing legitimate still uses them.

container.why: FORWARD chain is managed at the host level. Remove orphan rules on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo iptables -L FORWARD -n --line-numbers
   sudo iptables -D FORWARD N

nftables_parallel.title: nftables ruleset active in parallel with UFW (iptables backend)
nftables_parallel.why: UFW writes its rules to the iptables backend. If nftables is also active with its own ruleset, two firewall stacks evaluate every packet — and the order of evaluation depends on kernel version, module load order, and the netfilter compatibility layer. The result is non-deterministic packet processing: a port `ufw allow` opens may be silently dropped by an nftables rule, or vice versa. Symptoms are intermittent connectivity failures that look like network bugs but are firewall ones.
nftables_parallel.how:
1. Inspect the nftables ruleset:
   sudo nft list ruleset
2. Decide which stack you want to keep:
   - Keep UFW → flush nftables and disable its service:
     sudo nft flush ruleset
     sudo systemctl disable --now nftables
   - Switch to nftables → uninstall UFW and reconfigure rules natively in nftables:
     sudo ufw disable
     sudo apt purge ufw
3. Persist whichever choice you made (netfilter-persistent for iptables/UFW, nftables.conf for nft).

server.why: On a server, two parallel firewall stacks produce intermittent connectivity bugs that are very hard to diagnose. Pick one stack and remove the other; consistency is more important than the specific choice.

desktop.why: On a desktop, parallel stacks usually surface as 'sometimes this service is reachable, sometimes it is not'. Pick one and stick with it.

container.why: Firewall stack is host-level; this affects all containers. Reconcile on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo nft list ruleset
   sudo nft flush ruleset           # if keeping UFW
   sudo systemctl disable --now nftables

ip_forward_enabled.title: IP forwarding enabled but no routing daemon detected (Docker / libvirt / WireGuard absent)
ip_forward_enabled.why: net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 turns the host into an IP router — it will forward packets between interfaces according to its routing table. Docker, libvirt/KVM and WireGuard legitimately enable this for guest / VPN traffic, but none of those are running. Unexplained IP forwarding usually means a removed VPN or virtualisation package left the sysctl set, or it was enabled manually for debugging and never reverted. An unused forwarding host can be abused as a routing relay if the FORWARD chain is permissive.
ip_forward_enabled.how:
1. Disable IP forwarding immediately:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0
2. Make it permanent — edit /etc/sysctl.conf or a file under /etc/sysctl.d/ and set:
   net.ipv4.ip_forward=0
3. Re-apply sysctl settings:
   sudo sysctl --system
Note: if you later install Docker, libvirt or WireGuard, those packages will re-enable forwarding automatically. The fix above is only for the current state.

server.why: On a non-routing server, ip_forward=1 with no daemon is dormant attack surface. Either install the daemon that explains why forwarding is needed, or disable forwarding.

desktop.why: A desktop is virtually never a router. Forwarding enabled without a VPN or virtualisation daemon is leftover state — disable it.

container.why: ip_forward is a host kernel setting; it cannot be changed from inside a default container. Apply on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0
   echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf

duplicate_found.title: Duplicate or redundant UFW rules
duplicate_found.why: Duplicate firewall rules do not improve security but add confusion and maintenance overhead. Redundant rules make the policy harder to audit and can cause unexpected behaviour when rules are later modified or deleted, since UFW processes rules in order.
duplicate_found.how:
1. List rules with numbers:
   sudo ufw status numbered
2. Identify and delete the redundant rule:
   sudo ufw delete <number>
3. Verify the remaining ruleset:
   sudo ufw status verbose

open_any_found.title: Open wildcard rule (ALLOW from Anywhere to Anywhere)
open_any_found.why: A rule allowing all traffic from anywhere to anywhere negates the entire firewall for the affected port or protocol. This is equivalent to having no firewall at all — any external host can reach any open service.
open_any_found.how:
1. Identify the wildcard rule:
   sudo ufw status numbered
2. Delete it:
   sudo ufw delete <number>
3. Replace with specific rules covering only the required sources and ports:
   sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 22
4. Confirm the default policy is deny:
   sudo ufw default deny incoming

ipv6_missing.title: IPv4 rules present but no equivalent IPv6 rules
ipv6_missing.why: If a service is reachable over both IPv4 and IPv6 but only IPv4 is covered, the IPv6 path is completely unfiltered. An attacker using IPv6 bypasses all the firewall rules that appear to protect the service. This asymmetry is a common blind spot.
ipv6_missing.how:
1. Ensure /etc/default/ufw has IPV6=yes
2. UFW rules added without specifying a protocol apply to both IPv4 and IPv6 automatically:
   sudo ufw allow 22/tcp  # creates both v4 and v6 rules
3. Check which services listen on IPv6:
   sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':::'
4. Reload UFW:
   sudo ufw reload

clamav.db_outdated: Virus database is {days} day(s) old — consider updating

ntp.not_enabled_detail: Without NTP, the system clock drifts over time. Enable systemd-timesyncd (lightweight, built-in) or chrony (more accurate, recommended for servers).

container_security.privileged: Container is PRIVILEGED — the full Linux capability set is available ({caps})
container_security.privileged_detail: A privileged container can largely act as root on the host — it is the most common container-escape path. Every capability the kernel knows is in the bounding set, and seccomp is usually disabled with it. Drop what you do not need: --cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=<only what the workload requires>, and avoid --privileged unless the workload genuinely manages the host.

container_security.rootfs_writable: Root filesystem is writable — consider a read-only rootfs (--read-only) with explicit writable volumes
container_security.cap_sys_admin: CAP_SYS_ADMIN granted — not a privileged container, but the most escape-prone capability ({caps})
container_security.cap_sys_admin_detail: CAP_SYS_ADMIN alone permits mount, pivot_root and much of what root does on the host; it is widely described as "the new root". This container does NOT hold the full capability set, so it is not privileged — but a single targeted grant is enough for most documented escapes. It is often added for FUSE mounts or nested containers; check whether the workload still needs it, and prefer a narrower capability if one exists.
